Thus these element-to-homology maps, even for all powers and all finite-cover lifts, do not recognize a discrete conjugacy class. The construction supplies an element of \(G\); it does not supply the Galois automorphism and compatible full transporter required in E.2.22.

Let \(F=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle\) be a specified discrete free group of finite rank, and put \(G=\widehat F\). For each open normal subgroup \(N\subset G\), set \[ \begin{aligned} K_N&=F\cap N,& A_N&=K_N/[K_N,K_N],\\ D_N&=\overline{[K_N,K_N]}^{\,G},& \Gamma_N&=F/[K_N,K_N],\\ P_N&=G/D_N,& Q_N&=G/N=F/K_N. \end{aligned} \tag{E.2.28a} \] The group \(\Gamma_N\) embeds in \(P_N\). Define the actual subgroup and its displayed inverse-limit realization by \[ \mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}} =\bigcap_N\pi_N^{-1}(\Gamma_N)\subset G, \qquad \mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\simeq\varprojlim_N\Gamma_N, \quad \pi_N:G\longrightarrow P_N. \tag{E.2.28b} \] For an open subgroup \(U\subset G\), write \(\Lambda_U=(F\cap U)^{\mathrm{ab}}\subset U^{\mathrm{ab}}\). This is the integral homology lattice of its actual finite cover of the bouquet of \(r\) circles. For a continuous automorphism \(\alpha\) of \(G\), the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item The actual induced map \(U^{\mathrm{ab}}\to \alpha(U)^{\mathrm{ab}}\) carries \(\Lambda_U\) onto \(\Lambda_{\alpha(U)}\) for every open \(U\). \item The same assertion holds on the integral lattices \(A_N\) for one characteristic cofinal chain of open normal subgroups. \item There is one element \(h\in G\) such that \((\operatorname{ad}(h)\alpha)(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}) =\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\). \end{enumerate} Furthermore, an actual continuous automorphism \(\beta\) of \(G\) preserves \(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\) if and only if \(\beta(x_j)\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\) for \(1\leq j\leq r\). For the punctured curve of E.2.22 this characterizes preservation of all \emph{affine} integral homology lattices, up to one actual inner adjustment. Passing from the proper-homology condition in E.2.22 to this affine condition requires the vanishing of the boundary-extension classes identified below. The discrete-representative and Galois requirements remain open.

Let \(U=\mathbb P^1_{\overline{\Q}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\), fix \(F=\langle X,Y\rangle=\pi_1^{\mathrm{top}}(U(\mathbb C))\), and specify the quotient \[ \pi:\widehat F\longrightarrow H=A_5,\qquad X\longmapsto x=(123),\quad Y\longmapsto y=(12345). \tag{E.2.29a} \] Products of permutations act as compositions of functions. Let \(Y_H\to U\) be its actual connected Galois cover, let \(C_H\) be its smooth compactification, and put \[ \begin{aligned} L&=H_1(Y_H(\mathbb C),\Z),\\ P&=\langle\text{oriented boundary classes}\rangle\subset L,\\ W&=H_1(C_H(\mathbb C),\Z)=L/P . \end{aligned} \] There is an actual continuous automorphism \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(\widehat F)\) with \(\pi\alpha=\pi\) and \(\alpha^{\mathrm{ab}}=1\) such that its action on \(\ker(\pi)^{\mathrm{ab}}=\widehat L\) is the completion of an integral \(H\)-equivariant automorphism \(\gamma\) of \(L\), but \(\gamma(P)\not\subset P\). In particular this action does not induce an endomorphism of the fixed proper-homology quotient \(W\). The construction has \[ g(C_H)=9,\quad \#(C_H\setminus Y_H)=44,\quad \operatorname{rank}L=61,\quad \operatorname{rank}P=43,\quad \operatorname{rank}W=18 . \tag{E.2.29b} \] It supplies an integral matrix \(N\), an actual boundary class \(b\in P\), and an integral functional \(q:L\to\Z\) with \[ N^2=0,\quad \gamma=I+60N,\quad q(P)=0,\quad qNb=19440,\quad q\gamma b=1166400 . \tag{E.2.29c} \] The same failure holds for every positive power of \(\alpha\). This is a statement about one specified cover. It gives no simultaneous transporter of the proper integral lattices in E.2.22; its failure to preserve the actual cusp module also excludes it from the Galois image.

Let \(F=\langle x,y\rangle\) be the specified topological fundamental group of \(X=\mathbf P^1(\C)\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\), put \(z=(xy)^{-1}\), and put \(G=\widehat F\). For every open normal subgroup \(N\subset G\), let \(Y_N\) be the actual regular cover, let \(C_N\) be its smooth compactification, and define \[ \begin{aligned} K_N&=F\cap N,& A_N^c&=H_1(C_N,\Z),\\ L_N&=\ker(K_N\longrightarrow A_N^c),& J_N&=\overline{L_N}^{\,G},\\ \Gamma_N^c&=F/L_N,&P_N^c&=G/J_N,& Q_N&=G/N. \end{aligned} \tag{E.2.30a} \] There are actual embeddings and inverse-limit identifications \[ \Gamma_N^c\hookrightarrow P_N^c=\widehat{\Gamma_N^c}, \qquad \mathcal H_c:=\bigcap_N(\pi_N^c)^{-1}(\Gamma_N^c) \simeq\varprojlim_N\Gamma_N^c\subset G, \quad \pi_N^c:G\longrightarrow P_N^c. \tag{E.2.30b} \] The subgroup \(\mathcal H_c\) is self-normalizing in \(G\). Let \(\alpha\) be an actual continuous automorphism of \(G\) that permutes the three peripheral conjugacy classes and sends each specified peripheral generator to a conjugate of a unit power of the corresponding generator. For an open subgroup \(U\subset G\), write \(C_U\) for the compactification of its actual cover and \(\Lambda_U^c=H_1(C_U,\Z)\). The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item The actual induced completed proper-homology map carries \(\Lambda_U^c\) onto \(\Lambda_{\alpha(U)}^c\) for every open \(U\subset G\). \item It carries \(A_N^c\) onto itself on one characteristic cofinal chain of open normal subgroups. \item There is one \(h\in G\) with \((\operatorname{ad}(h)\alpha)(\mathcal H_c)=\mathcal H_c\). \end{enumerate} For any one such \(h_0\), all aligning conjugators are exactly \[ \{h\in G:h\alpha(\mathcal H_c)h^{-1}=\mathcal H_c\} =\mathcal H_c h_0. \tag{E.2.30c} \] For a peripheral-preserving automorphism \(\beta\), the condition \(\beta(\mathcal H_c)=\mathcal H_c\) is equivalent to the two memberships \(\beta(x),\beta(y)\in\mathcal H_c\). Moreover, \[ \mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\subsetneq\mathcal H_c, \qquad x^{\widehat\Z},\ y^{\widehat\Z},\ z^{\widehat\Z} \subset\mathcal H_c. \tag{E.2.30d} \] Applied to the actual Galois automorphisms in E.2.22, this is an exact description of the proper-lattice premise. It does not establish the affine boundary-extension vanishing of E.2.28 or a discrete representative for the actual Galois action.

Retain the actual groups \(F=\langle x,y\rangle\), \(G=\widehat F\), and \(\mathcal H_c\subset G\) of E.2.30. There is a specified element \(f\in G\) such that \[ f^{-1}yf\in\mathcal H_c, \qquad f\notin\mathcal H_c C_G(y). \tag{E.2.31a} \] Its specification below uses the actual \(A_5\)-cover of E.2.29, an explicit invariant proper homology class, and integral transfer along a fixed cofinal cover tower. Thus membership of one conjugated cusp generator does not force its conjugator to lie in \(\mathcal H_c\) times the cusp centralizer. No assertion is made that this \(f\) defines an automorphism preserving all three peripheral classes or occurs as the conjugator of an arithmetic Galois automorphism.

Let $X/\C$ be smooth and proper, and let $z$ be an integral algebraic cycle of codimension $p$. Choose $i$ and orient each complex coordinate line by $(1,i)$. In ordinary, untwisted cohomology, \[ c_X\bigl(P_{\mathrm{alg}}(z)\bigr)=(2\pi i)^pP_{\mathrm{top}}(z), \qquad \alpha_X\bigl(P_{\mathrm{top}}(z)\bigr)=(2\pi i)^{-p}P_{\mathrm{alg}}(z). \tag{F.1.1} \] The equality holds with supports before passing to ordinary cohomology. The integral topological group maps to complex cohomology through its quotient by torsion.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper morphism of smooth complex algebraic varieties, of pure dimensions $d,e$, and put $p=e-d$. The cohomological Gysin maps have types \[ f_*^{\B}:H^r(X,\C)\to H^{r+2p}(Y,\C),\qquad f_*^{\dR}:H^r_{\dR}(X)\to H^{r+2p}_{\dR}(Y). \] With the residue-normalized de Rham trace, \[ \alpha_Y f_*^{\B}=(2\pi i)^{-p}f_*^{\dR}\alpha_X. \tag{F.1.2} \] This includes negative $p$, and is compatible with composition. It proves the degree shift and scalar of 18:23 for $r=2i$ as well as for odd $r$.

Let $X,Y/\C$ be smooth proper, $d=\dim X$, and $z\in\operatorname{CH}^r(X\times Y)$. Put $t=r-d$. The two untwisted actions are \[ z_*^{\B}(x)=p_{2*}^{\B}(p_1^*x\,P_{\mathrm{top}}(z)),\qquad z_*^{\dR}(x)=p_{2*}^{\dR}(p_1^*x\,P_{\mathrm{alg}}(z)), \] from degree $m$ to degree $m+2t$. They satisfy \[ \alpha_Yz_*^{\B}=(2\pi i)^{d-r}z_*^{\dR}\alpha_X. \tag{F.1.3} \] Consequently comparison is compatible with the degree-zero correspondence action ($r=d$), and with the general action after the target is written $H^{m+2t}(Y)(t)$.

Let $k$ be an abstract field isomorphic to $\C$, let $X/k$ be smooth, and choose an isomorphism $\sigma:\C\to k$, in the direction written on 18:19. Set $X_\sigma=X\otimes_{k,\sigma^{-1}}\C$. The transported Betti cycle class in $H^{2p}_{\dR}(X/k)$ is \[ P^{(p)}_\sigma=\sigma(2\pi i)^{-p}P_{\mathrm{alg}}. \tag{F.1.4} \] Changing $\sigma$ to $\sigma c$, with $c$ complex conjugation, multiplies this class by $(-1)^p$ and preserves the whole embedded integral Betti lattice (modulo torsion). Different complete archimedean topologies can give different lattices, already for $\mathbf P^1$.

In the one-dimensional line $H^1(\mathbf P^1_K,\Omega^1)=Kv$, as complete archimedean topologies and the accompanying orientation choices vary, the comparison images of an oriented integral generator are exactly \[ \{a v:a\in K\text{ is transcendental over }\Q\}. \tag{F.1.5} \] For a fixed one of these lattices the primitive elements are its two generators. Without a lattice, ``primitive'' has no specified meaning. The reading ``all possible'' is correct for the displayed set of comparison generators; the reading ``every nonzero vector of $Kv$'' is false.

For a smooth proper variety $X/\R$, set $L=H^r(X(\C),\Z)/\mathrm{torsion}$. Integral Betti--etale comparison and Betti--de-Rham comparison embed $L$ diagonally in \[ \left(\prod_\ell H^r_{\mathrm{et}}(X_\C,\Z_\ell)/\mathrm{torsion}\right) \times \bigl(H^r_{\dR}(X/\R)\otimes_\R\C\bigr). \] The image is stable under $\Gal(\C/\R)$, acting on the first factor by geometric Galois action and on the second by coefficient conjugation. This is the integral assertion C08 on 18:29.

For an integral or rational mixed Hodge structure $E$, using increasing $W$ and decreasing $F$, \[ W_i(E(n))=W_{i+2n}(E)\otimes\Q(n),\qquad F^a(E(n))=F^{a+n}(E)\otimes\C, \] with the evident integral tensor line in the integral case. Consequently \[ \operatorname{Gr}_i^W(E(n))= \bigl(\operatorname{Gr}_{i+2n}^W E\bigr)(n). \tag{F.2.1} \] In particular the index in $\operatorname{Gr}_i^W(E(-1))$ is $i-2$ on the right.

Let $k$ be perfect of characteristic $p$, including $p=2$, and let $A/k$ be an abelian variety. In Oda's contravariant, left-Dieudonne-module convention there is a canonical isomorphism \[ M(A[p])\xrightarrow{\sim}H^1_{\dR}(A/k). \] It identifies $VM(A[p])$ with $H^0(A,\Omega_A^1)$ and the quotient with $H^1(A,\mathcal O_A)$, and hence identifies their exact sequences. This resolves the characteristic-$p$ extension question in I.P04 and II.RH18 in precisely this abelian scope.

On the primitive string $V_m=\bigoplus_{j=0}^m\Q v_j$, put \[ Ev_j=v_{j+1},\quad \Lambda v_j=v_{j-1},\quad Fv_j=j(m-j+1)v_{j-1},\quad Hv_j=(2j-m)v_j, \] with zero at the endpoints. Then \[ [E,F]=H,\qquad[H,E]=2E,\qquad[H,F]=-2F. \] On $W=\bigoplus_{m=0}^dV_m$ the actual operator subalgebras satisfy \[ \Q[E,\Lambda]=\Q[E,F,H] =\prod_{m=0}^d\operatorname{Mat}_{m+1}(\Q). \] On the displayed integral string of length two, however, \[ \Z[E,F,H]\ne\Z[E,\Lambda]=\operatorname{Mat}_3(\Z). \] These prove the exact rational assertions of II.MB03--MB03b and refute their unqualified integral extension for this lattice.

For a smooth projective $d$-fold, on $H^i(X)$ put $w_X(t)=t^i$ and $\lambda_X(t)=t^{i-d}$. Then $\lambda_X(t)=t^{-d}w_X(t)$, and both conjugate a degree-$j$ operator by $t^j$. For the character $\varepsilon$ on $\Q(-1)$, the tensor weight gives $\varepsilon w=t^2$. A filtration splitting with $\varepsilon j=t$ is a separately specified map. The displayed Lefschetz representation on $H^*(\mathbf P^1)$ does not factor through the Tate representation $\rho(z)=\operatorname{diag}(1,z)$, but satisfies \[ \rho(z)E\rho(z)^{-1}=zE,\qquad \rho(z)F\rho(z)^{-1}=z^{-1}F. \] The map $E:h^0\to h^2(1)$ is equivariant. On elliptic $H^1$ the Lefschetz Lie-algebra action is zero, so it is not the nonzero standard action of the normalized period $\SL_2$ there.

For a neutral rigid abelian $\Q$-linear tensor category $\mathcal C$ with exact faithful fibre functor $\omega$, the tensor-automorphism construction gives an equivalence \[ \mathcal C\xrightarrow{\sim}\Rep_\Q\bigl(\Aut^\otimes(\omega)\bigr), \] and tensor-isomorphisms between fibre functors form the corresponding torsor. With compatible Betti fibre functors and a fixed $\Qb\subset\C$, rational Nori motives have the exact affine-group-scheme sequence \[ 1\longrightarrow G_{\mathrm N}(\Qb) \longrightarrow G_{\mathrm N}(\Q) \longrightarrow\underline{\Gal(\Qb/\Q)}\longrightarrow1. \] For a field embedded in $\C$ and a principal ideal coefficient domain, the specified Ayoub and Nori Betti motivic Hopf algebras are isomorphic by the constructed inverse maps. The pure rational Nori category is equivalent to Andre's motivated category. General Nori Hodge fullness remains the explicitly stated conjectural obligation; fullness on the abelian-generated pure category over $\C$ is established.

The identity on algebraic cycles induces the surjection \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{hom}}(M,N) \twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{num}}(M,N). \] Rational numerical motives are semisimple. A cohomology realization factors through this quotient exactly when its kernel acts trivially; on the relevant smooth projective products this is numerical equals homological equivalence for the correspondence classes. Semisimplicity does not imply a trivial centre. Nor does a normalized group $\SL_2$ with a surjection to the Tate torus determine the full group: $(\GL_2,\det)$ and $(\Gm\times\SL_2,\operatorname{pr}_1)$ have that kernel and are not isomorphic. Their explicit comparison is the central isogeny $(q,A)\mapsto qA$, which squares the specified Tate character.

Mochizuki's sub-$p$-adic Hom theorem concerns dominant maps and open continuous arithmetic fundamental-group homomorphisms, modulo geometric inner automorphisms. For proper curves, the induced linear comparison is geometric pro-$\ell$ abelianization followed by the Albanese identification with the Tate module of the Jacobian. Tate's finite-field and Faltings's number-field Hom theorems govern the resulting abelian-variety maps. For a centre-free geometric group, the arithmetic extension is recovered as the pullback of $\Aut\to\operatorname{Out}$ along its outer Galois action. For proper real hyperbolic curves, section classes recover connected real components, but their conjugation actions on geometric abelianization coincide. Stix's cusp-inertia criterion requires the non-Tate-weight condition, an open arithmetic normalizer image, and the specified cyclotomic character action.

The equality of $H^*(X(\R),\Q)$ with the conjugation invariants in $H^*(X(\C),\Q)$ is false, including the unrestricted degree-zero reading. The raw Weil-element centralizer in $G(\R)$ need not be compact. In the polarizable real category of C.1.1, after quotienting a finite tensor-generator group by the central weight image, the centralizer of the Weil element is maximal compact. The two-element normalizer written in the cancelled paragraph then equals that centralizer.

For $X$ smooth over a discrete valuation ring $R$, there is an integral specialization ring homomorphism \[ \operatorname{sp}:\operatorname{CH}^*(X_\eta) \longrightarrow\operatorname{CH}^*(X_s) \] which sends a prime cycle to the special fibre of its flat closure, with its scheme-theoretic multiplicities. For $R$ complete, $X$ smooth proper, and $\ell$ invertible in $R$, the map on geometric fibres commutes with the integral $\Z_\ell$ cycle-class map under the proper smooth specialization isomorphism. This retains torsion and answers the stated DVR version of I.P07--P08.

At an isolated transverse intersection with a codimension-$p$ subvariety of a smooth complex $n$-fold, a smooth transversal has dimension $p$. The frozen dimension label $n-p$ in I.P28 has that value only when $n=2p$.

The complete LM6 A.50 proves descent of a \emph{power} of a normalizer character. Its noncuspidal alternative produces a weight-one Jacobian character; it does not supply the cyclotomic-action premise needed to close LM6 A.22. The previously unavailable full statement and proof have now been read. Their first Sylow-subgroup step is valid after the explicit enlargement $N\mapsto NA$ below.

An arbitrary automorphism-indexed abstract semilinear action does not always arise from algebraic descent, even on an affine finite \emph{\'etale} scheme with two geometric points. This closes the unqualified reading in II.P16.02; it does not affect the actual fpqc tensor-Isom construction in II.P16.01.

Fix an integral tensor fibre functor $\omega_0$ and put $\mathcal G=\Aut^\otimes(\omega_0)$. Its fppf-local tensor forms are classified by $\mathcal G$-torsors through \[ [\omega]\longmapsto [\Isom^\otimes(\omega_0,\omega)]. \tag{F.3.12a} \] For affine finite-type $\mathcal G$ over $\Z$, this is a finite set. More generally the same conclusion holds over the ring of $S$-integers of a number field for a finite set $S$. No connectedness, reductivity or smoothness of $\mathcal G$ is needed for this statement. Over these Dedekind rings all fpqc-local forms are already fppf-local, without a flatness assumption on $\mathcal G$, and the same finiteness applies. An unrestricted proalgebraic version is false.

Let $R$ be noetherian, let $\mathcal C$ be a small rigid symmetric $R$-linear exact tensor category, and let $\omega:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Proj}_f(R)$ be an exact faithful tensor functor. Fix an object $M$ from which every object of $\mathcal C$ is obtained, up to isomorphism, by finitely many direct sums, tensor products, duals, and admissible subobjects and quotients. For an $R$-algebra $A$, put $\omega_A(X)=\omega(X)\otimes_R A$. Restriction to $M$ represents the functor \[ A\longmapsto\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}(\omega_A) \] by a closed subgroup scheme of $\operatorname{GL}_R(\omega M)$, hence by an affine group scheme of finite presentation over $R$. For $R=\mathcal O_{F,S}$, with $F$ a number field and $S$ a finite set of finite primes, the isomorphism classes of fpqc-local tensor forms of this particular $\omega$ are consequently finite, by the explicit torsor equivalence and Dedekind-ring approximation in F.3.12. No smoothness, flatness, connectedness or reductivity of the resulting automorphism scheme is needed.

Every smooth integral projective $d$-fold $X$ over a characteristic-zero field $k$ admits a finite birational morphism \[ \nu:X\longrightarrow Y\subset\mathbf P_k^{d+1} \] onto an integral hypersurface, and $\nu$ identifies $X$ with the normalization of $Y$. This is an actual geometric construction relevant to the proposed use of singular hypersurfaces. Let $k$ be any commutative ring, including rings with torsion, and let $M,N$ be arbitrary $k$-modules. A homogeneous polynomial law $f:M\rightsquigarrow N$ of degree $d\geq0$ means a family of maps \[ f_R:R\otimes_k M\longrightarrow R\otimes_k N \qquad(R\in\operatorname{CAlg}_k) \] natural in the commutative $k$-algebra $R$, with $f_R(rx)=r^d f_R(x)$. It is not merely its function $f_k$ on $k$-points. There is a natural isomorphism of $k$-modules \[ \operatorname{Pol}^d_k(M,N) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Gamma^d_k M,N). \tag{A1.1} \] Here $\Gamma^d$ is the degree-$d$ part of the universal divided-power algebra; $\Gamma^0 M=k$, $\Gamma^1M=M$. The isomorphism sends $u$ to $(1\otimes u)\gamma_{d,R}$. Divided powers commute with arbitrary scalar extension and satisfy \[ \Gamma^d(M\oplus N)\simeq \bigoplus_{a+b=d}\Gamma^a M\otimes_k\Gamma^b N. \tag{A1.2} \] The exact references are Roby, Theorem IV.1, pp.~266--267, Theorem III.3, p.~262, and Theorem III.4, pp.~262--263 \cite{Roby1963}. We opened these statements and their surrounding definitions. No projectivity or characteristic restriction occurs in these results. For nonflat modules one must use the universal divided-power construction, not silently replace it by invariant tensors.

Let $\mathsf P_k$ be the category of finitely generated projective $k$-modules. The divided-power category used for strict polynomial functors has the same objects and \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma^d\mathsf P_k}(V,W) =\Gamma^d\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,W). \tag{A1.5} \] Its composition preserves the fixed degree $d$ and is bilinear. Its linear representations $\Gamma^d\mathsf P_k\to\operatorname{Mod}_k$ are strict polynomial functors of degree $d$. This is Krause, \S2, especially the definition on p.~3 and Remark~2.2 on pp.~4--5 \cite{Krause2013}; over a field it is equivalent to Friedlander--Suslin, Definition~2.1 and Lemma~2.2, \S2 \cite{FriedlanderSuslin1997}. It is false that the manuscript's $\mathcal P_d(V,W)$ is (A1.5). The correct relation is that a degree-$d$ polynomial-law action on \emph{linear Hom modules}, compatible with identities and composition as laws, is represented by (A1.5), and therefore defines such a linear representation. The degree-$p$ divided-power functor is one example, as proved in A1.4. The category $\mathcal P_k$ itself is the category of bounded polynomial laws, not a fixed-degree divided-power category and not the category of its representations.

This answers scan~86 affirmatively for its principal example over \emph{every} commutative ring, without finite generation or a base-change isomorphism for Hom.

Its image is open. More precisely, let $S$ contain the finite primes occurring in the principal ideals of the $\xi_j$. In the finite free abelian group $U_S=\mathcal O_{K,S}^{\times}/\mu(K)$, let $H$ be the lattice generated by the classes of the $\xi_j$, let $H^{\mathrm{sat}}=(H\otimes\mathbb Q)\cap U_S$, and choose a positive integer $e$ annihilating $H^{\mathrm{sat}}/H$. Put $D=e|\mu(K)|$. Then \[ D\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{r} \subseteq\rho(\Gamma_{K(\mu_\infty)}) \subseteq\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{r}. \] In particular the total index is at most $[\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}:\chi(\Gamma_K)]D^r$. For $r=0$ this is simply the cyclotomic openness statement. For $r\geq2$ the image is not open in the larger group $\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{r}\rtimes\operatorname{GL}_r(\widehat{\mathbb Z})$. If the $\xi_j$ are not rational, the acting group must be $\Gamma_K$ for a field containing them; a separate permutation action must be specified before replacing it by $\Gamma_{\mathbb Q}$.

\label{A1.1} Suppose that $Z$ is a regular Hausdorff space and $Y\subset Z$ is closed. The inverse limit in $\Topos$ of the open subtopoi $\Sh(N)\subset\Sh(Z)$, for $N$ ranging over all neighborhoods of $Y$, is $\Sh(Y)$. The analogous limit of $\Sh(N\setminus Y)$ is the empty topos. Thus taking this limit before gluing discards precisely the punctured-neighborhood information.

\label{A1.2} For every tuple $\alpha=(N_i)_{i\in I}$ of open neighborhoods $N_i\supset X_i$ in $X$, put \[ W_i^\alpha=N_i\setminus R_i^{\mathrm{ord}},\qquad C_q^\alpha=\Sh\left(\coprod_{(i_0,\ldots,i_q)\in I^{q+1}} W_{i_0}^\alpha\cap\cdots\cap W_{i_q}^\alpha\right). \tag{A.1.4}\label{eq:tubecech} \] The $W_i^\alpha$ form an open cover of $X$. Their augmented Cech diagram has the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item For every fixed $\alpha$, its truncation in degrees $0,1,2$ has $\Sh(X)$ as its bicolimit in $\Topos$. \item Regard each $C_q=(C_q^\alpha)_\alpha$ as a \emph{single synchronized pro-object}. Then \[ \mathop{\mathrm{bicolim}}_{[q]\in\Delta_{\leq2}^{\mathrm{op}}}C_q \simeq c\Sh(X) \quad\text{in }2\Pro(\Topos). \tag{A.1.5}\label{eq:procech} \] \item If $I$ is finite, one can equivalently use the individual nonempty intersections $W_A=(\Sh(\bigcap_{i\in A}W_i^\alpha))_\alpha$ for $1\leq |A|\leq3$, with all their face inclusions. For infinite $I$, the synchronized pro-coproducts in (\ref{eq:tubecech}) are part of the assertion; no interchange of an infinite product and a filtered colimit is asserted. \end{enumerate} No Thom--Mather, Whitney, or homotopy-link assumption is needed. Such assumptions are needed for geometric models and homotopy replacements of the intersections, not for this descent theorem.

\label{A1.3} The successor-pair diagram of 151/069 does not have $\Sh(X)$ as its colimit. Even the diagram of \emph{all} manuscript pair and triple stones, with \emph{all} their canonical inclusions over $X$, does not suffice. Both assertions fail for the Whitney and conically smooth stratification \[ X=\mathbb C,\qquad X_0=\{0\},\quad X_1=\mathbb R,\quad X_2=\mathbb C. \] Disconnected open strata are allowed, as in the question. The all-pair and all-triple failure also has a connected-stratum example in $\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$, described below.

\label{A1.4} For ordinary-topos open-cover descent, vertices, pair overlaps, and triple cocycles are the smallest universal Cech arities. In the subset-indexed presentation of A1.2(3), each vertex, pair, or triple intersection object can be indispensable for an appropriate finite open cover; intersections of four or more members are unnecessary. There is no claim that every slot of every particular cover is indispensable. Ordered repetitions and degeneracies in the full Cech diagram are not being counted as independently necessary pieces. In binary gluing, the three-piece span $\Sh(N)\leftarrow\Sh(N\cap U)\to\Sh(U)$ is universally indispensable; an extra soul $\Sh(Y)\to\Sh(N)$ with no other incidence is redundant.

\label{A1.5} Let $X$ be a $T_1$ space, $C$ a small category, and $D:C\to\operatorname{Open}(X)$ a diagram of open subsets and inclusions. For $x\in X$, let $C_x$ be the full subcategory on the objects $c$ with $x\in D(c)$. The canonical cocone has $\Sh(X)$ as its bicolimit if and only if the groupoid obtained by inverting every arrow of $C_x$ is equivalent to the terminal groupoid, for every $x$. Equivalently, each $|N(C_x)|$ is nonempty, connected, and simply connected. This gives an exact test for any proposed deletion of objects or arrows from a specified honest-open gluing diagram. An inclusion-minimal subdiagram is precisely one satisfying this test for which every further permitted deletion fails the test at some point.

\label{A2.1} Let $f:Z'\to Z$ be continuous and $Y\subset Z$ closed. The canonical comparison from the neighborhood pro-object of $f^{-1}Y$ in $Z'$ to the pullback of $\mathcal N_Z(Y)$ is an isomorphism over $Z'$ if the family $\{f^{-1}N:N\supset Y\text{ open}\}$ is cofinal among neighborhoods of $f^{-1}Y$. Equivalently, for every closed $F'\subset Z'$ disjoint from $f^{-1}Y$, there is an open $N\supset Y$ with $f^{-1}N\cap F'=\varnothing$. This holds for every closed continuous map $f$, in particular for proper maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces. No local-immersion hypothesis is necessary.

\label{A2.2} Open immersions do not generally satisfy A2.1. Moreover, formula (4) of 151/071 for the support-based $R_{ij}$ fails under arbitrary inverse images, even for a closed immersion. The order-based definition (\ref{eq:Riord}) does commute with every inverse image.

\label{A2.3} Descent for a specified open-cover diagram is local on $X$: restrictions of that cover to an open cover of $X$ verify the same gluing equivalence, and these local equivalences glue. The argument proposed and retracted in 151/072 is invalid when it replaces the pullback of a closed-center pro-neighborhood by the independently recomputed neighborhood system on an open subset.

\label{A3.1} Let $I''\subset I'\subset I$ be lower ideals, and put $Z=X_{I''}$, $X'=X_{I'}$, $U=X'\setminus Z$. The induced strata of $U$ are exactly the $S_i$ with $i\in I'\setminus I''$. For retained $i,j$, passing from $X$ to the closed union $X'$ preserves the pair stones defined inside $X_j$ (with fixed order-based deletions, or nonempty strata). Passing to $U$ need not preserve even their number of connected components or their homotopy types, including in the conically smooth Whitney example of A1.3.

\label{A3.2} For an open union of strata $j:U\hookrightarrow X'$, restriction $j^*: \Sh_{\mathrm{c}}(X')\to\Sh_{\mathrm{c}}(U)$ is essentially surjective and has the fully faithful extension-by-empty left adjoint $j_!$. It is an equivalence exactly when $Z=X'\setminus U$ is empty. Its full reconstruction is the recollement with $\Sh_{\mathrm{c}}(Z)$ and the nearby-section functor of B.1, with its constructibility conditions.

\label{A4.1} Under a)--d), the strata $S_i$ partition $X$, and the colimit of the closed-subset diagram $i\mapsto X_i$, equivalently the coequalizer of its flag diagram, is $X$ as a topological space. Empty strata may be discarded without destroying a)--d).
\label{A4.2} A finite meet-semilattice diagram of closed embeddings need not embed its members in its colimit, even if its associated ordered space satisfies (23a)--(23b) of 151/053.

\label{A4.3} For a finite diagram of closed embeddings indexed by a finite poset, all maps to its topological colimit are closed embeddings if and only if no zigzag of transition identifications identifies two distinct points in one member. If $I$ is a finite meet-semilattice, the stronger condition \[ X_{i\wedge j}\xrightarrow{\sim}X_i\times_{X_k}X_j \quad(i,j\leq k) \tag{A.4.1}\label{eq:cartesianmeet} \] is sufficient, and then the intersection of the images of $X_i,X_j$ in the colimit is exactly the image of $X_{i\wedge j}$.

\label{A4.4} Under a)--d) with nonempty strata, the strengthened condition (24) of 151/054 is equivalent to the family of closed subsets $\{X_i\}$ being closed under binary intersection, with the intersection represented by one index. The conditional version, requiring infima only for pairs with a common lower bound, is equivalent to this assertion for nonempty intersections. The literal all-pairs version additionally needs a bottom index representing the empty intersection whenever disjoint closed strata occur.

\label{A4.5} Let $2g-2+n>0$, and order isomorphism classes of connected stable graphs of genus $g$ with $n$ individually labelled legs by reverse contraction: $H\leq G$ if $H$ contracts to $G$. Every pair having a common lower bound has an infimum exactly for \[ g=0\ (n\geq3),\qquad g=1\ (1\leq n\leq3),\qquad (g,n)=(2,0). \tag{A.4.2}\label{eq:smallgn} \] Consequently the conditional interpretation of Lead L4 and the quoted EXIT\_TOWER A.2 is correct. Literal (24) requires the empty-bottom qualification of A4.4. This statement concerns graph types, not fixed contractions or the incidence category.

Let $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed inclusion of topological spaces and let $j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X$ be its complementary open inclusion. There is an equivalence \[ \operatorname{Sh}(X)\simeq \{(L,E,\alpha):L\in\operatorname{Sh}(U),\ E\in\operatorname{Sh}(Y),\ \alpha:E\longrightarrow i^{-1}j_*L\}. \tag{B1.1} \] Morphisms on the right are pairs of sheaf morphisms commuting with $\alpha$. Its restriction to the full subcategory $\mathcal F$ of sheaves locally constant on $U$ and $Y$ is obtained by imposing $L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U)$ and $E\in\operatorname{Loc}(Y)$. No normal triviality, local contractibility, separation, or finiteness assumption is needed for this statement.

Suppose in addition that $N\subset X$ is an open neighbourhood of $Y$ with a retraction $r:N\to Y$, and write $N^*=N\setminus Y$ and $p=r|_{N^*}:N^*\to Y$. For $L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U)$ there is a natural germ comparison \[ \theta_L:p_*(L|_{N^*})\longrightarrow i^{-1}j_*L. \tag{B1.3} \] Indeed a section over $p^{-1}W$ gives a germ along the open subset $W\subset Y$ by using the neighbourhood $r^{-1}W$. If every $\theta_L$ is an isomorphism, then \[ \mathcal F\simeq \{(L,E,\varphi):L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U),\ E\in\operatorname{Loc}(Y),\ \varphi:p^{-1}E\longrightarrow L|_{N^*}\}. \tag{B1.4} \] More generally, without assuming (B1.3) to be an isomorphism, the precise necessary and sufficient condition for this functor of systems to be an equivalence over the fixed pair $(L,E)$ is that \[ \operatorname{Hom}_Y(E,p_*(L|_{N^*}))\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_Y(E,i^{-1}j_*L) \tag{B1.5} \] be bijective. Requiring the description after restriction to every open subset of $Y$, and for every locally constant $E$, makes the isomorphism condition on (B1.3) necessary as well as sufficient.

The assertion on 151/035 is false if, without normal or neighbourhood stability hypotheses, a map on a pro-tube means a morphism represented on one sufficiently small neighbourhood. This fails even for a compact metric $X$ with two strata, one a point and the other a disjoint union of one-dimensional manifolds.

In the connected case let $D=\pi_1(N^*)$, $B=\pi_1(Y)$ and $G=\pi_1(U)$, with homomorphisms $p_*:D\to B$ and $i_*:D\to G$. Assume $p_*$ is onto and put $I=\ker p_*$. Then (18) of 151/036 is equivalent to the $B$-equivariant map \[ E\longrightarrow (i_*^*L)^I. \tag{B1.6} \] Indeed a $D$-equivariant map from a $D$-set on which $I$ acts trivially has image in the $I$-fixed points, and the induced action on those fixed points factors through $D/I=B$. Conversely such a $B$-map is $D$-equivariant. If $p$ is a fibration with connected fibre $K$, its homotopy exact sequence gives \[ \pi_2(Y)\longrightarrow\pi_1(K)\longrightarrow D \longrightarrow B\longrightarrow1. \tag{B1.7} \] Thus $I$ is the quotient of $\pi_1(K)$ by the image of the connecting homomorphism, and it equals $\pi_1(K)$ only when that homomorphism is zero. This independently rechecks R4, SA10-C3-04. If $Y$ and $K$ are aspherical, the same long exact sequence gives $\pi_q(N^*)=0$ for $q\geq2$. Disconnected fibres are handled by the groupoid formulation; surjectivity of $D\to B$ must not then be silently asserted.

We give a criterion that does not assume a chosen retraction or a stationary representative. Let $\mathcal N_Y$ be the filtered ordered set of open neighbourhoods of $Y$, with arrows given by shrinking. Form the filtered bicategorical colimits in categories \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal T&=\operatorname*{2colim}_{N\in\mathcal N_Y} \operatorname{Loc}(N),\\ \mathcal T^*&=\operatorname*{2colim}_{N\in\mathcal N_Y} \operatorname{Loc}(N\setminus Y). \end{aligned} \tag{B1.8} \] Their objects and arrows have representatives on one neighbourhood; two representatives agree if they agree after a common shrinking. There are restriction functors $r:\mathcal T\to\operatorname{Loc}(Y)$, $a:\mathcal T\to\mathcal T^*$, and $b:\operatorname{Loc}(U)\to\mathcal T^*$. For $E\in\mathcal T$ and $L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U)$, restriction of a representative morphism to germs along $Y$ defines \[ \mu_{E,L}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T^*}(aE,bL) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{Y}(rE,i^{-1}j_*L). \tag{B1.9} \] The natural functor from systems $(L,E,\varphi:aE\to bL)$ to $\mathcal F$ is an equivalence, compatible with restriction to $U$ and $Y$, if and only if both of the following conditions hold: $r$ is an equivalence, and every map (B1.9) is bijective. These are respectively an extension condition for local systems and a uniform extension condition for their gluing morphisms. For a cofinal system of actual tube retractions, B1.2 supplies sufficient geometric hypotheses for both conditions.

Let $\mathcal S$ be the $\infty$-category of spaces and $\operatorname{Top}_\infty$ the $\infty$-category of $\infty$-topoi and geometric morphisms. The shape $\Pi_\infty\mathcal X\in \operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal S)$ is characterized by \[ \operatorname{Map}(\Pi_\infty\mathcal X,K) \simeq \Gamma_{\mathcal X}\Delta_{\mathcal X}K, \qquad K\in\mathcal S. \tag{B2.1} \] For every small diagram whose colimit in $\operatorname{Top}_\infty$ is $\mathcal X$, the canonical map \[ \operatorname*{colim}_a\Pi_\infty\mathcal X_a \longrightarrow\Pi_\infty\mathcal X \tag{B2.2} \] is an equivalence of pro-spaces. No stratification or normal fibration hypothesis occurs here.
The same sentence is false if ``colimit of topoi'' means a bicategorical colimit of ordinary Grothendieck topoi, and the right side means a homotopy colimit of their shapes.

For a metric space $X$ and a closed subset $Y$, put \[ H=\operatorname{holink}(X,Y) =\{\gamma:[0,1]\to X:\gamma(0)\in Y, \ \gamma(t)\notin Y\ (t>0)\}. \] The maps $e_0:H\to Y$ and $e_1:H\to U$ are endpoint evaluations. If $Y$ is forward tame in $X$, then the ordinary homotopy types satisfy \[ X\simeq Y\mathbin{\cup^h}_{H}U. \tag{B2.4} \] Quinn proves a controlled strict relative version in \cite[Lemma 2.4(2)]{Quinn1988}, using his controlled holink and mapping-cylinder convention. We give a separate proof of (B2.4) that does not identify that cylinder topology with the ordinary quotient-cylinder topology. Let $N$ range over the open neighborhoods of $Y$. The numerable open cover $X=N\cup U$ gives, naturally in $N$, the homotopy-pushout equivalence $N\cup^h_{N\setminus Y}U\simeq X$. A fixed tame deformation gives an equivalence $\{N\}_N\simeq\operatorname{const}Y$ in prospaces: for any target neighborhood $N$, shrink to the points whose entire deformation lies in $N$. The same fixed deformation and the explicit endpoint-preserving path homotopy of C4.02 give $\{N\setminus Y\}_N\simeq\operatorname{const}H$. Those formulas need only tameness of this pair; the fibration part of the HSS definition is not used. The comparison uses the natural zigzag through paths wholly contained in $N$, so its endpoint maps and the homotopy between the two maps to $X$ are the original ones. The finite span colimit in $\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal S)$ is computed on these synchronized levels, because filtered colimits of spaces commute with finite simplicial limits. Replacing the two pro-germs by their constant equivalents therefore gives $\operatorname{const}X\simeq \operatorname{const}(Y\cup^h_HU)$. The constant embedding is fully faithful, proving (B2.4). In the usual quotient double-cylinder model, the associated map to $X$ is induced by the continuous path evaluation $H\times[0,1]\to X$. Quinn's Definition 3.1 adds, for each incident pair of strata, that $e_0$ is a fibration. That is the precise normal-fibration analogue of 151/032, once a deleted tube has been compared with the holink. It is not the whole definition: forward tameness remains a separate hypothesis. The fibration condition alone does not imply tameness. For the Hawaiian earring with $Y$ its common point, $e_0$ is a fibration because its target is a point. But $Y$ is not tame: a neighbourhood deformation into $Y$ would null-homotope every sufficiently small circle in $X$, while retraction of $X$ onto any one of those circles shows its fundamental loop is nonzero. Consequently L2 must be read with this additional tameness and comparison data, and its unrestricted topos-colimit conclusion must be replaced by B2.1. The shape theorem itself needs neither condition.

For $(\mathbb C,\{0\})$, B1.4 identifies a constructible sheaf with a set $E$, a $\mathbb Z$-set $M$, and a map $E\to M^{\mathbb Z}$. Equivalently it is a covariant set-valued functor on the category with objects $p,q$, automorphism group $\mathbb Z$ at $q$, and a unique map $p\to q$. The object $p$ is initial; hence the classifying space of this category, and the shape of its functor topos, is contractible. This agrees with $\mathbb C$. For $(S^2,\{p\})$, the complementary plane is contractible. The same description reduces to a single map of sets $E\to M$. The corresponding arrow category also has contractible classifying space. Nevertheless the genuine tube span has shapes \[ *\longleftarrow S^1\longrightarrow *, \] whose homotopy pushout is $\Sigma S^1\simeq S^2$. Thus the ordinary constructible-sheaf topos does not retain the sphere's higher homotopy type. This proves the assertions SA10-C3-05 and SA10-C3-06 without identifying that functor topos with the required higher gluing.

Assume that $X$ is paracompact, locally of singular shape, and conically stratified by a poset $P$ satisfying the ascending chain condition. These hypotheses hold, for example, for a finite-dimensional, paracompact Hausdorff topologically stratified space with the compact conical charts used in \cite[Definition 3.1]{Treumann2009}. Write $\operatorname{Exit}(X)=\operatorname{Sing}_P(X)$. For every integer $n\geq0$ there are equivalences \[ \begin{split} \operatorname{Cons}_{\leq n}(X) &\simeq \operatorname{Fun}(\operatorname{Exit}(X),\mathcal S_{\leq n})\\ &\simeq \operatorname{Fun}(h_{n+1}\operatorname{Exit}(X), \mathcal S_{\leq n}). \end{split} \tag{B3.1} \] Here the left side consists of constructible $n$-truncated sheaves of spaces, and $h_{n+1}$ retains the objects and the $n$-truncations of all mapping spaces, with their coherent compositions. The regularity hypotheses on the strata are substantive. If ``conical'' only means a local product with a cone, allowing an arbitrary unstratified base, every one-stratum space is conical. The Cantor-space example after B1.3 then refutes the unqualified claim already at $n=0$, and also at every higher level by regarding sets as discrete spaces. For the usual finite Thom--Mather, Whitney, or conically smooth spaces with manifold strata, the hypotheses used here hold. Disconnected and empty strata cause no change: the statement is componentwise and an empty stratum contributes no objects.

At $n=1$, (B3.1) is the equivalence between constructible stacks in groupoids and homotopy-coherent $2$-functors from the exit-path $2$-category to groupoids. It is also the restriction of \cite[Theorem 7.14]{Treumann2009} from category-valued to groupoid-valued stacks: the value at each object is the stalk category, so the condition that these values are groupoids is preserved in both directions. His Theorem 7.13 proves compatibility with open-cover descent. The set-valued level, by contrast, is $n=0$: it retains $\pi_0$ of each exit mapping space. Thus L3's phrase ``truncated at $\pi_1$ of the links'' is one level too high if it means that link $\pi_1$ survives as automorphisms of exiting arrows. Those automorphisms first appear in the stack level. For $(S^2,\{p\})$, the two-stratum exit category can be represented by two objects and cross mapping space $S^1$: the open stratum is contractible, and its attaching holink has the homotopy type of $S^1$. Taking $\pi_0$ makes a single arrow, while the fundamental groupoid of that mapping space retains $\mathbb Z$. This is exactly the difference seen by the gerbes. One should also distinguish two uses of gluing. A general constructible stack is a closed--open system (B3.2), with a possibly noninvertible functor to nearby data. An $A$-banded gerbe is locally equivalent to $BA$ at every point of $X$. Its gluing over an honest open tube and $U$ uses an \emph{equivalence} on their overlap, as in 151/042. These gerbes form a subproblem of the constructible-stack theorem; arbitrary constructible stacks are not all gerbes.
Let $A$ be any discrete abelian group with constant band. Then \[ H^2(S^2;A)\cong A. \tag{B3.4} \] We obtain this by the precise gluing on 151/041--043.

For a two-stratum homotopy-pushout decomposition $X\simeq Y\cup^h_H U$, suppose every component of $Y,H,U$ is a $K(\pi,1)$ of CW homotopy type. Then the diagram \[ \Pi_1Y\longleftarrow\Pi_1H\longrightarrow\Pi_1U \tag{B4.1} \] \emph{does} determine the full weak homotopy type of $X$: \[ X\simeq B\Pi_1Y\mathbin{\cup^h}_{B\Pi_1H}B\Pi_1U. \tag{B4.2} \] No extra invariant is required for this span. Thus R5 does not establish the insufficiency asserted in the last sentence of B.4.

Let $X\to P$ satisfy the hypotheses of B3.1, and put $\mathcal E=\operatorname{Exit}(X)$. For every nonempty strict chain $\sigma=(p_0<\cdots<p_m)$ in $P$, define \[ D(\sigma)=\operatorname{Map}_{/P}(\sigma,\mathcal E). \tag{B4.3} \] This is a space: a natural transformation over the fixed chain has components inside strata, hence all its components are equivalences. Restriction along subchains defines a homotopy-coherent functor $D:\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal S$. Without any asphericity assumption, the complete assembly formula is \[ \operatorname{Sing}(X)\simeq \operatorname*{colim}_{\sigma\in\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}} D(\sigma). \tag{B4.3a} \] Assume that every stratum $D(p)$ and every total incidence link $D(p<q)$ is a $1$-type. Then the groupoids \[ G_\sigma=\Pi_1D(\sigma), \qquad G:\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gpd}, \tag{B4.4} \] with \emph{all} restriction functors and their coherent comparison isomorphisms determine the full homotopy type: \[ \operatorname{Sing}(X)\simeq \operatorname*{colim}_{\sigma\in\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}} BG_\sigma. \tag{B4.5} \] The colimit in (B4.5) is taken in spaces, not in ordinary groupoids. The incidence-link hypothesis holds when the local homotopy links are aspherical and their source maps are fibrations over aspherical strata. In geometric applications, ``all links'' must mean all incident pairs, not merely adjacent pairs or a union of different link strata.

The trivial circle bundle $S^2\times S^1\to S^2$ and the Hopf bundle $S^3\to S^2$ have locally the same aspherical pieces and the same maps on fundamental groups over a good cover. Their gluing coherences differ, and their total spaces have different fundamental groups.

\label{b5.1.-the-forest-statement-and-the-full-condition} \textbf{Status: Proved.} Hyp 1, 2 and \(2'\) of 151/011--014 are respectively the epimorphicity of \[L(1)\to1,\qquad L(ya\times yb)\to U_a\times U_b,\] and \[L(ya\times_{yc}yb)\to U_a\times_{U_c}U_b\] for every cospan \(a\to c\leftarrow b\) in \(A\). These are equivalent to \(c_F\) being epic for all diagrams indexed by the free category on a finite oriented forest, including the empty forest. This is an equivalence with a collection of tests; it does not assert that every indexing category which is not a forest fails. For example, a category with an initial object has its limit given by evaluation there.
\label{b5.2.-a-finite-counterexample} \textbf{Status: Refuted, corrected by B5.1.} Hyp 1, 2 and \(2'\) neither imply full (Hyp) nor suffice for homotopy descent over a point.

\label{b5.3.-the-symmetric-group-nerve-distinguish-three-realizations} \textbf{Status: Proved, with a correction to ambiguous uses of realization.} Let \(\mathsf F\) be nonempty finite sets and all maps, \(A=\mathsf F^{\mathrm{op}}\), and \(G\) a discrete group. Put \(U(S)=G^S/G\) for simultaneous left multiplication. Hyp 1, 2 and \(2'\) hold, and \[\operatorname{hocolim}_{\mathsf F^{\mathrm{op}}}U\simeq BG.\] For \(G\ne1\), full (Hyp) fails. The ordinary simplicial restriction also realizes to \(BG\). In contrast, the literal symmetric coend realization with affine simplices is contractible for finite \(G\).

\label{b5.4.-classification-of-flat-symmetric-systems} \textbf{Status: Proved.} Flat functors \(\mathsf F^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal X\) are exactly the systems \(S\mapsto E^S\) with \(E\to1_{\mathcal X}\) epic. In sets, \(E\) is a nonempty set.

\label{b5.5.-flatness-forest-comparisons-and-verdier-hypercovers} \textbf{Status: Refuted for the proposed ``strictly between'' description.} A hypercover condition agreeing with Verdier's cannot in general lie between the manuscript's forest conditions and flatness. For \(A=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\), the ordinary Cech nerve \(U_n=\{0,1\}^{n+1}\) of a cover of a point is a hypercover, and its realization is the contractible nerve of the indiscrete groupoid on two objects. Yet Hyp \(2'\) fails. Take in \(\Delta\) the span \([0]\leftarrow[1]\to[2]\), with the first map constant and the second selecting endpoints 0,2. The corresponding fiber product contains \((0,(0,1,0))\). A cocone must have a monotone map \([2]\to[m]\) with equal endpoint values, hence a constant map. Every tuple lifted from a completing cone is therefore constant in those three positions. The displayed element has no lift. In particular full (Hyp) fails as well. Conversely, \(\Delta[1]\) is a flat functor on \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\): its extension is evaluation at \([1]\). It is not a hypercover of a point, because its degree-one matching map omits the ordered pair of vertices \((1,0)\). Thus even flatness and Verdier's condition are incomparable for ordinary simplicial indexing. The failure of ``between'' persists for symmetric indexing. Put \(U(S)=\operatorname{Cont}(\Delta(S),\mathbf R)\), with maps by affine precomposition. Every continuous boundary map to \(\mathbf R\) extends to the simplex by coning from the barycenter and interpolating to zero; compactness gives continuity at the barycenter. Hence the ordinary simplicial restriction is a hypercover of a point. For the finite-set span \(1\leftarrow2\to3\), with the right map selecting vertices 0,2, take zero on \(\Delta^0\) and \[b(t_0,t_1,t_2)=t_1(t_0-t_2).\] They agree on edge 02. Any amalgamating finite-set map identifies vertices 0,2, so its affine map takes \((1/2,1/2,0)\) and \((0,1/2,1/2)\) to the same point. A lifted function must have equal values there; \(b\) has values \(1/4,-1/4\). Thus Hyp \(2'\) fails. Exact rational computation checks this obstruction on 30 amalgams; the argument proves it for every target cardinality. There is nevertheless a one-way implication specific to symmetric indexing: full (Hyp) implies the hypercover condition. By B5.4 its system is \(U(S)=E^S\) with \(E\to1\) epic. The simplicial restriction is the Cech nerve of this epimorphism; every positive matching map is an isomorphism. The symmetric continuous-simplex example just given proves the converse false. Thus ordinary flatness and hypercovers are incomparable, whereas symmetric flatness is strictly stronger than hypercovers; in either case hypercovers need not satisfy the forest conditions. Over sets there is also an explicit ordinary-index classification: flat functors \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}\) are precisely nerves of nonempty linear orders. Indeed a flat functor is a filtered colimit of the covariant representables \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}}([n],-)=\Delta[n]\). A filtered colimit of finite ordinals and monotone maps is a linear order: comparisons and antisymmetry are witnessed at a common stage. The same complete procedure gives \[ (c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3)=(74,132,57,4),\qquad (s_0,s_1,s_2)=(288,576,267). \] All $288$ vertex links are four-cycles, all closed faces embed, and the quotient is connected and non-orientable. Thus this surface is $\#^{23}\mathbb{RP}^2$, with Euler characteristic $-21$. The independent axiom check makes $928\,233$ signed basis-exchange checks. Together with C.04, this proves that the topology is not a function of $n$ alone. \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{lrrrrrr} \hline Input & $c_0$ & $c_1$ & $c_2$ & $c_3$ & $s_0$ & $s_2$\\ \hline Three lines & 4 & 6 & 0 & 0 & 12 & 10\\ Four convex dual points & 12 & 18 & 3 & 0 & 36 & 33\\ Five convex dual points & 31 & 50 & 15 & 0 & 100 & 96\\ Six convex dual points & 74 & 132 & 57 & 4 & 288 & 267\\ Six-line input C.02 & 80 & 150 & 75 & 10 & 360 & 315\\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{center} The first three rows reproduce the earlier small cases and extend the test to one five-line input. They are not substituted for a claim about arbitrary arrangements.

\label{C.06} For the particular realization C.02, the fifteen dual lines have $42$ ordinary double vertices, one ordinary triple vertex at $p=(0,0,1)$, and six supercritical vertices of multiplicity five. Exact cross products give \[ V=49,\qquad E=42\cdot2+3+6\cdot5=117,\qquad F=1-V+E=69. \] The non-supercritical \emph{straight} positions therefore number $(V-6)+E+F=229$, and their sector count is $2E=234$. Their corresponding surface has Euler characteristic $-5$. These counts are independently produced by \texttt{counts\_straight\_dual.py} using integer arithmetic. They do not equal the pseudoline counts $315$ and $360$. Stretchability after moving the original lines cannot identify all pseudoline extensions with straight extensions of a fixed realization. In particular, around the displayed triple position there are eight topological stable resolutions, while the fixed straight realization supplies only six angular sectors.

\label{C.07} If a non-supercritical pseudoline $D$ passes through $\nu$ vertices of a nontrivial arrangement of $n$ distinct pseudolines, then $2\nu\le n$. Each such vertex uses at least two original lines; no original line can occur at two different vertices on $D$, because it would meet $D$ twice. The sets of original lines used at those vertices are therefore disjoint. This proves the inequality and shows that $n=6$ is the first possible size for a three-vertex position. C.02 realizes this bound.

Lead L2 is false: all $2^\nu$ stable generizations are present in $\mathcal X$. Its true replacement is the following explicit cellular description. Subdivide every ordinary cube of $\overline T(M)$ by its coordinate midplanes. Its vertices are the centers of the original cube faces, hence ordinary extension labels; its edges are the ordinary cover relations. Replace each parallel polygon by the M\"obius band of E4, subdivided as described below. In this CW model of $B(M)$ the dual quadrangulation $\mathcal X^\vee$ is an embedded subcomplex containing the entire one-skeleton. Specifically, if $\sigma$ has distinct zero coordinates $i,j$ and resolving them with specified signs gives $\sigma_i,\sigma_j,\sigma_{ij}$, its diamond is \[ \sigma<\sigma_i<\sigma_{ij},\qquad \sigma<\sigma_j<\sigma_{ij}. \] The associated quadrangle is the union of these two closed order-complex triangles. It occurs in the ordinary part of the dual manuscript map exactly when the specified transition ports at $i,j$ are adjacent in the full boundary cycle of its disk. This construction specifies the ordinary quadrangles and their attaching maps. The exceptional part consists of the entire subdivided M\"obius bands. Their rectangular cells are indexed by the original flags $(v,e)$, and their four vertices are $U_e^+,S_v^+,S_v^-,U_e^-$ in that cyclic order. Thus there are specified comparison maps \[ \mathcal X\cong\mathcal X^\vee \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ }B(M) \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }\overline T(M). \] Here $\iota$ is a cellular subcomplex inclusion and induces a surjection on fundamental groups; $\beta$ is the continuous blow-down collapsing each inserted M\"obius core circle to its parallel point. The inclusion $\iota$ is a homotopy equivalence exactly when no ordinary position passes through three old vertices. In that case it is an identification of the indicated CW spaces.

A cyclic signed word $W$ is the deployed boundary polygon of a non-supercritical relative position for the prescribed $\Sigma$ if and only if the following finite tests hold, with the calibration just specified: \begin{enumerate} \item $\chi_{q_W}$ satisfies the unsigned basis axiom and \eqref{eq:P-GP}; \item no row of $q_W$ is identically zero; \item $W$ agrees, up to a cyclic shift, with $\operatorname{Exp}_M(q_W)$. \end{enumerate} If $W$ is given without a cyclic orientation, perform these steps with either orientation; the resulting extension is taken modulo reorientation of $d$. The tests include arbitrary vertex multiplicities and any number of vertices on $d$.

The $2n$ weight rule, the cluster-reversal rule, and the presence of at least three empty-triangle candidates, even tested against every old line by \eqref{eq:P-triangle}, do not characterize the image. This fails for a simple arrangement of six straight lines. The complete replacement is P4, or equivalently the localization criterion together with the prescribed packet expansion.

For a fixed labelled nontrivial arrangement $\Sigma$, its full image of deployed polygons determines all non-supercritical relative positions, all ordinary specialization arrows, their directions and weights, and their cyclic incidences at each position. Adjoining the known $n$ supercritical positions recovers the corridor arrows and their weights. Together with the prescribed transition transport used in constructing the surface, these data determine its cellularly embedded weighted graph, up to label-preserving isomorphism of cellular maps. The reconstructed graph alone does not assert that every face has order four; that is the separate local-link assertion of A.1.

Let $\Delta$ be a closed disk, with finitely many labelled tame proper arcs $\delta_i$ whose $2n$ endpoints on $\partial\Delta$ are distinct. Suppose each pair meets at most once, at an interior transverse crossing, and disjointness together with equality is an equivalence relation on the arcs. If there are at least two equivalence classes, this system is the cut-open system of a projective pseudoline arrangement and an added pseudoline. If there is just one class, the same assertion holds exactly when its endpoints form two consecutive packets, each containing one endpoint of each chord. The reconstructed old arrangement is nontrivial exactly when its pairwise intersection points are not all the same point.

For the fixed labelled nontrivial arrangement $\Sigma$, the map from non-supercritical relative positions to literal deployed signed polygons is injective. The polygon determines the rank-two contraction by the signed pair-alternation rule, including all its parallel classes. The only ambiguity is reorientation of the added element, corresponding to reversal of the chosen cyclic orientation.

If the vertices of $\Sigma$ on $d$ have line clusters of sizes $k_1,\ldots,k_\nu$, the deployed word consists of paired consecutive packets in opposite order. Let $H$ be the half-turn on the $2n$ positions and let $R$ reverse the order separately within every packet, fixing singleton packets. The label-negation involution is $H\circ R=R\circ H$. It equals $H$ exactly when $d$ is stable. The within-packet order is \eqref{eq:P-expansion}.

Let $d$ be a non-supercritical relative position through distinct old vertices $v_1,\ldots,v_
u$. Resolving any chosen subset to either local side can be performed independently. The resulting generizations are indexed by $\{0,+,-\}^{
u}$, where zero means unresolved, and the $2^
u$ fully resolved positions are distinct. In particular two distinct chosen vertices give four distinct positions in each ordinary commuting square.

Suppose that a non-supercritical new pseudoline $d$ passes through exactly one old vertex $v$. On the spherical double cover, let $\alpha$ be either open semicircle of $d$ between the two lifts of $v$. Choose an old line $i$ through $v$ adjacent to $d$ on one side, and let $L$ be the closed lune bounded by $\overline\alpha$ and the corresponding semicircle of $i$. If $L$ contains an old vertex in its interior, then an empty specialization fan has its base in $\alpha$. If it contains no old interior vertex, $d$ is in the corridor position next to $i$ on that side. In particular, a half-circle between its generization ports contains an ordinary specialization or is an exceptional corridor half-circle.

The literal identification in L4 is false. The additional arc datum described for an interior lieu on cote 156-4/032 has an interior end and an end on the boundary. A chord of R1 has both ends on the boundary. These are different types of embedded arc, even in an ordinary disk. The exact elementary relationship is the following: a proper chord together with a marked interior point splits into two boundary tethers with a common interior end and disjoint interiors; conversely, two such tethers with distinct boundary ends glue uniquely to a proper chord. For families, the pairwise single-crossing and parallel-class conditions of R1 must still be imposed separately.

For every compact definable $B$, the simplicial group of automorphisms \[ (b,t)\longmapsto(b,h(b,t))\quad\text{of }B\times[0,1] \] is contractible when $h(b,0)=0$ and $h(b,1)=1$. For every compact definable $Y$, the simplicial group of homeomorphisms of the closed cone $CY$ fixing both its base $Y$ and its vertex $o$ is contractible. These prove the fibrewise form of 119/148 I c) and 119/149 II c), respectively; they do not prove I c) for arbitrary automorphisms.

Suppose a compact definable pair $(X,B)$ admits a strict collar. The simplicial space $\operatorname{Col}^{\mathrm{rig}}(X,B)$ of all strict collar embeddings is contractible. This verifies the collar-space portion of Lead L1 with the stated family convention. It is distinct from contractibility of rigidifications of one fixed image.

Let $B=(S^1)^d$, $d\geq6$, with its finite semialgebraic PL model. For $\mathrm{CAT}=\mathrm{PL}$ or $\mathrm{TOP}$, put \[ P_{\mathrm{CAT}}(B)= \Homeo_{\mathrm{CAT}}(B\times[0,1]\,;B\times\{0\}). \] Then \[ \pi_0P_{\mathrm{CAT}}(B) \cong \F_2[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_d^{\pm1}]/\F_2\{1\} =\bigoplus_{v\in\Z^d\setminus\{0\}}\F_2. \] The same component computation holds for definable concordances of this model in every o-minimal expansion of a real closed field. In particular we may take $B=(S^1)^6\subset K^{12}$, given by the six equations $x_i^2+y_i^2=1$.

Let $B$ be any closed definable manifold and choose its finite PL model, with the closed-manifold convention including definable compactness. Inclusion gives a natural isomorphism \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(B)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_0P_{\rm def}(B). \] These component groups are independent of the ordered field used to realize the finite PL model. Over the real field, if every component of $B$ has dimension at least five, the map of simplicial groups $P_{\rm PL}(B)\to P_{\rm TOP}(B)$ is a weak equivalence. Thus for general $K$ the definable component group also agrees with the TOP component group of a chosen real realization of the finite PL model in that range. We do not claim a canonical map from a non-Archimedean realization to the real TOP space. The last statement does not assert a weak equivalence with the whole definable concordance group.

For $B=(S^1)^6$, the automorphism space in 119/148 I c) is not contractible. Moreover the boundary-collapse functor from bordant pairs to pointed spaces is not a Dwyer--Kan equivalence in the stipulated definable simplicial categories. Its map on automorphism spaces at $(B\times[0,1],B\times\{0\})$ has homotopy fibre equivalent to $P_{\mathrm{def}}(B)$. Therefore the full cascade of 119/150 and Lead L1 cannot be repaired by rigidifying collars alone.

Use strict collars and strict conical neighborhoods, and require morphisms to preserve the chosen product or cone parametrizations. Then \[ PBCR\simeq EPCR\simeq EPC. \] The first is an equivalence induced by collapsing the lower collar boundary and blowing up the cone vertex. The second is a weak equivalence on every mapping space and is essentially surjective. These assertions hold with any finite number of disjoint labeled boundary pieces or points. They do not imply equivalence with $EP$.

Use parametrizable families for the unparametrized collar simplicial set: a simplex is a strict collar family admitting a parametrization, with no parametrization retained. If $(X,B)$ admits a collar, then \[ \operatorname{Col}(X,B)\simeq BP_{\mathrm{def}}(B). \] In particular 119/148 I b) is false for $B=(S^1)^6$: $\pi_1\operatorname{Col}(X,B)\cong\pi_0P_{\mathrm{def}}(B)\ne0$. The rigidified assertion A.102 and the fibrewise assertion A.101 are the precise different assertions that remain true.

Let $B$ be closed in a definable subset $X$ of an affine space over a real closed field. If $B$ has a finite definable local collar atlas, then there is a definable open collar $B\times[0,1)\to X$. If $X$ and $B$ are definably compact, it restricts after rescaling to a strict closed collar. Thus I a) holds for the compact bordant pairs used here.
Every compact definable pointed space $(X,o)$ admits a strict closed conical neighborhood of $o$, including when $o$ is isolated.

Let $F:PB\to PBCR$ attach $B\times[-1,0]$ to $X$ along $B\times\{0\}=B$, with new boundary $B\times\{-1\}$ and its displayed rigid collar. Let $K:PB\to EPCR$ attach $CB$ to $X$ along its base. Both functors are equivalences of the specified definable simplicial categories, with actual isomorphisms on mapping spaces. In particular the valid corrected comparison is \[ PB\simeq PBCR\simeq EPCR\simeq EPC. \] This conclusion does not include $EP$.

On $PB$ with all homeomorphisms, neither the collar-absorption isomorphism $UF\Rightarrow\id$ nor the cone-absorption isomorphism $VK\Rightarrow Q$ is a strict natural isomorphism. Here $U$ forgets the attached collar, $V$ forgets the attached cone, and $Q$ collapses the original boundary. They become strict natural isomorphisms after passing to pairs with a chosen extended collar and maps preserving its product coordinates. This is the role of the manuscript's marginal instruction to precompose with $PBR$ at 119/150.

For a simplicial category of homeomorphisms, define its derived space of choices over an object to be the homotopy fibre of the map on classifying spaces of its maximal simplicial groupoids. For $X=C B$ with $B=(S^1)^6$, the component of the standard strict cone in the derived space of strict conical neighborhoods of the vertex has homotopy type \[ BP_{\mathrm{def}}(B). \] Consequently II b) is false with this categorical interpretation of choice, and remains false for rigidified strict-cone choices. The space of rigidifications of a \emph{fixed} cone is contractible, as II c) asserts. These three assertions concern different spaces.

For the strict collar and strict cone conventions above, five of the eleven arrows are equivalences of the definable simplicial categories. The other six fail in the torus example of A.103. The following table distinguishes the two copies of $PB$ in the drawing by position. \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{p{0.58\linewidth}p{0.30\linewidth}} \toprule Arrow & Outcome\\ \midrule Top $PB\to PBCR$, attach a collar & equivalence (A.109)\\ Top $PB\to EPCR$, attach a cone & equivalence (A.109)\\ Top $PB\to$ bottom $PB$, identity & equivalence\\ Top $PB\to EP$, collapse & fails (A.104)\\ $PBCR\to EPCR$, collapse & equivalence (A.105)\\ $PBCR\to PBC$, forget product coordinates & fails\\ $EPCR\to EPC$, forget cone coordinates & equivalence (A.105)\\ $PBC\to EPC$, collapse & fails\\ $PBC\to PB$, forget the collar & fails\\ $EPC\to EP$, forget the cone & fails (A.111)\\ Bottom $PB\to EP$, collapse & fails (A.104)\\ \bottomrule \end{tabular} \end{center} Here ``fails'' means that the functor is not an equivalence in general; we do not assert failure at every bordant pair with that boundary.

Let $B$ be a closed compact PL manifold, and use total-space PL and definable families to define the respective simplicial concordance groups $P_{\rm PL}(B)\subset P_{\rm def}(B)$. In addition to the bijection on components in A.113, inclusion induces a surjection \[ \pi_1(P_{\rm PL}(B),\operatorname{id}) \longrightarrow \pi_1(P_{\rm def}(B),\operatorname{id}). \] More explicitly, every based definable circle family of concordances is based definably homotopic to a family that is PL as a map of total spaces. If the field is $\R$ and every component of $B$ has dimension at least five, this map on $\pi_1$ is an isomorphism. In that scope the inclusion is injective on every homotopy group. For $k\ge2$ there is the precise splitting \[ \pi_kP_{\rm def}(B)\simeq \pi_kP_{\rm PL}(B)\oplus \ker\bigl(\pi_kP_{\rm def}(B)\to\pi_kP_{\rm TOP}(B)\bigr). \]

Let $F\subset K$ be an extension of real closed fields and let $B$ be a closed compact PL manifold given by a finite polyhedral model over $F$. Extension of coefficients induces a weak equivalence of simplicial groups \[ P_{{\rm PL},F}(B)\longrightarrow P_{{\rm PL},K}(B_K). \] Consequently a fixed finite abstract PL model has the same PL concordance homotopy type over any two real closed fields, by the zigzag through a realization over the field of real algebraic numbers. This is a zigzag of coefficient-extension maps; it is not a literal map from a non-Archimedean field's families to ordinary topological families.

Let $F\subset K$ be real closed fields and let $B$ be a closed compact PL manifold given by a finite polyhedral model over $F$. Extension of coefficients induces a weak equivalence \[ P_{{\rm SA},F}(B)\longrightarrow P_{{\rm SA},K}(B_K), \] where families and their homotopies are semialgebraic maps of total spaces. The squares formed by these maps and the PL coefficient-extension maps commute. Thus the homotopy-group comparison $P_{\rm PL}\to P_{\rm SA}$ for a finite abstract PL model is independent of the real closed field and reduces to $\R$. In particular, if every component of $B$ has dimension at least five, then over every real closed field this comparison is bijective on components, is an isomorphism on $\pi_1$, and is injective on every homotopy group. Full weak equivalence is not asserted here.

Let $B$ be a closed connected PL manifold of dimension at least four, let $X=C_2B$ be its cone with radial interval $[0,2]$, and put $C=C_1B$. Give the locally flat outer faces of strict cone neighborhoods the local quotient topology from \[ \operatorname{Emb}_{\rm lf}\bigl(B,B\times(0,2)\bigr) /\Homeo(B), \] where embeddings have the compact-open topology and $\Homeo(B)$ acts by precomposition. An outer face determines the side containing the vertex. The component $\mathcal W$ of $C$ has weak homotopy type \[ \mathcal W\simeq BP_{\rm TOP}(B). \] For $B=(S^1)^6$, it is therefore not contractible. Its nontrivial loop can be chosen semialgebraic, and it cannot be filled by real definable families of strict cones whose outer faces admit local joint parameterizations. The same non-filling conclusion holds for finite semialgebraic simplex families with these joint semialgebraic witnesses over every real closed field. If an external parameterization $B\to\dot C$ is retained as part of each object, the component instead has weak homotopy type \[ B\Homeo\bigl(B\times[1,2]\ \mathrm{rel}\ B\times\{1,2\}\bigr). \] This is a different convention from the unparameterized outer faces in the preceding assertion.

Let $B$ be a closed definable manifold whose finite PL model $K$ is smoothable and has dimension at least $9$ on every component. The construction below, applied to each connected component of $K$, gives a countable abelian presentation $E(K)$ and an isomorphism \[ \pi_0P_{\rm def}(B)\cong E(K). \] The group operation on the right is addition of integral cycles. The presentation depends only on the finite simplicial homotopy model $K$, and is valid over every real closed field and every fixed o-minimal expansion. It also gives the stable smooth concordance component group for any compact smooth manifold, without a dimension restriction. It makes no unstable assertion for a nonsmoothable PL manifold or for an arbitrary manifold of dimension at most $8$.

Let $M$ be any compact PL manifold, with the side boundary fixed in the definition of concordance, and let $K$ be a finite simplicial homotopy model for $M$. The complete countable presentation $E(K)$ of A.119 computes its stable PL concordance component group: \[ \operatorname*{colim}_{j}\pi_0P_{\rm PL}(M\times I^j) \cong E(K). \] There is no smoothability or dimension hypothesis on this stable statement. It does not identify the unstable group with the stable group for a nonsmoothable PL manifold.

Let $M$ be a compact connected PL manifold of dimension $n\geq9$, possibly with boundary. All concordances fix the side boundary. Choose a finite combinatorial triangulation $K$ of $M$, and let $K^{(3)}$ be its $3$-skeleton. Then the countable abelian group presentation $E(K^{(3)})$ of A.119, including every cycle, boundary, and unit-image relation specified there, presents \[ \pi_0 P_{\rm PL}(M). \] No smoothing of $M$ is assumed. The same presentation gives the components of the stipulated definable concordance group of any compact definable manifold with this PL model, over any real closed field and in any fixed o-minimal expansion. Thus this is an unstable component computation, whereas A.120 computes the stable group in every dimension. The presentation is countable; no finite invariant factor decomposition or solution to its word problem is asserted. For a disconnected compact manifold, use the finite product of the presentations of its connected components.

Let $M$ be a compact connected PL manifold of dimension $n\geq6$, with any boundary fixed on the sides of a concordance, and let $K$ be a finite simplicial model of its homotopy type. Then \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(M)\cong E(K), \] where $E(K)$ is the complete countable group presentation of A.119. The same formula holds for the stipulated definable concordance group of a compact definable manifold with this PL model, over every real closed field and in every fixed o-minimal expansion. Use the product of these presentations for finitely many connected components, each of dimension at least six. More precisely, positive suspension induces an isomorphism on components of smooth concordance groups once $n\geq6$. This identifies the unstable group of a smoothable PL model with the stable presentation. The nonsmoothable PL case is obtained by localizing to a smoothable neighborhood of a $3$-skeleton, not by assuming a general unstable PL stability theorem. No assertion about arbitrary manifolds of dimensions four or five is included.

Let $P_{\rm PL}(B)$ fix $B\times\{0\}\cup\partial B\times I$ pointwise, with the upper face free. Then \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(B)=0 \] if $B$ is a compact manifold of dimension zero or one, if $B$ is a PL ball of any dimension, if $B$ is a compact orientable surface other than $S^2$, or if $B$ is a closed nonorientable surface other than $\mathbb{RP}^2$. The same assertion holds for a finite disjoint union of these manifolds and for their definable models over every real closed field, in the stipulated component convention. No higher homotopy-group assertion is made here. The two closed surfaces $S^2$ and $\mathbb{RP}^2$, and nonorientable surfaces with boundary, are not included in the surface clauses.

Let $M$ be a compact connected PL manifold of dimension five, possibly with boundary, and assume $\pi_2(M)=0$. For every finite connected pointed homotopy model $K$ of $M$, \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(M)\cong E(K), \] where $E(K)$ is the complete countable group presentation in A.119. The same calculation holds for the stipulated definable concordance components of any definable realization over a real closed field. It determines the full group, including its extension law; it is not a finite invariant-factor algorithm. There is no assertion here for five-manifolds with nonzero $\pi_2$, or for higher homotopy groups of the comparison.

For the standard PL two-sphere and every definable model of it over any real closed field, \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(S^2)=\pi_0P_{\rm def}(S^2)=0. \] Here the bottom is fixed pointwise and the upper boundary is free. This is a component assertion, not a higher parametric comparison.

Let $M$ be a closed connected PL five-manifold with $\pi_1M=0$. For any definable realization of its PL model over any real closed field, \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(M)=\pi_0P_{\rm def}(M)=0. \] There is no restriction on $\pi_2M$. The smooth input holds for closed simply connected smooth manifolds in every dimension at least five. Only the closed case of that input is invoked here.

For the standard PL projective plane and every definable model over any real closed field, \[ \pi_0P_{\rm PL}(\mathbb {RP}^2) =\pi_0P_{\rm def}(\mathbb {RP}^2)=0. \] The bottom is fixed pointwise and the top is free. Together with A.123 and A.125 this computes the component group for every closed surface. No higher parametric comparison is asserted.

For every standard PL sphere $S^n$, $n\geq2$, \[ \pi_0 P_{\mathrm{PL}}(S^n)=0. \] Consequently the same assertion holds for each definable model of the standard PL sphere over every real closed field, with the simplicial concordance convention of this study. In particular, this closes the standard $S^3$ and $S^4$ component cases without a smooth-to-PL comparison in base dimension three or four.

Let $M$ be a closed connected simply connected PL three-manifold. Then \[ \pi_0P_{\mathrm{PL}}(M)=0. \] The same holds for the stipulated definable concordance group of every closed definably simply connected definable three-manifold over a real closed field.

Let $B$ be a closed connected orientable PL three-manifold with infinite fundamental group. There is a group monomorphism \[ \bigoplus_{j\ge1}\mathbb Z\ \hookrightarrow \pi_0P_{\mathrm{PL}}(B). \tag{A.130.1} \] The same holds for its definable realizations over every real closed field. Over the real field, these classes remain independent after forgetting to topological concordances, even after further forgetting the fixed-bottom condition. This is a subgroup result, not a presentation of the entire three-dimensional concordance component group.

Let $K$ be a nonempty finite abstract simplicial complex whose realization is a closed PL manifold. The ordered finite list of simplices of $K$ is all the input in the following construction. There are explicit countable simplicial groups \[ G^{\mathrm{PL}}(K),\qquad G^{\mathrm{SA}}(K) \tag{A.131.1} \] with the following effective properties. Their simplices are finite integer strings; membership, equality, and degeneracy are decidable. Multiplication, inversion, faces and degeneracies are given by total algorithms. The construction also gives a computable simplicial homomorphism $G^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)\to G^{\mathrm{SA}}(K)$. For every real closed field $R$, coefficient extension gives weak equivalences \[ G^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)\longrightarrow P_{\mathrm{PL},R}(|K|_R), \qquad G^{\mathrm{SA}}(K)\longrightarrow P_{\mathrm{SA},R}(|K|_R), \tag{A.131.2} \] where the source is realized over the real algebraic numbers. All families are homeomorphisms of the total product with the parameter simplex, preserve that entire parameter, fix the bottom pointwise, and preserve the free top setwise. For each $r\ge0$, the algorithm in the proof outputs a complete countable presentation $\Pi_r^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)$, respectively $\Pi_r^{\mathrm{SA}}(K)$, for the entire homotopy group \[ \pi_rP_{\mathrm{PL},R}(|K|_R),\qquad \pi_rP_{\mathrm{SA},R}(|K|_R). \tag{A.131.3} \] For $r\ge1$ these groups are based at the identity; translation identifies the corresponding groups on any other component. Here ``outputs'' means that one uniform algorithm enumerates all specified generators and relators. For $r\ge1$ it may instead enumerate an integer relation matrix for the abelian group. For an arbitrary fixed o-minimal expansion, $\Pi_0^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)$ also presents the stipulated definable component group. If every component of $|K|$ has dimension at least five, (A.131.1) gives a weak model for the real TOP concordance space as well, and $\Pi_r^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)$ presents its homotopy groups for all $r$. For the empty complex and empty base, take the constant one-element simplicial group; every component and homotopy group is trivial. These are complete effective countable presentations and whole simplicial models. No terminating word problem, finite presentation, finite invariant-factor description, or efficient complexity bound is asserted. No higher weak equivalence from PL to SA or to an arbitrary o-minimal expansion is inferred.

Give the topological homeomorphism groups the compact-open topology, and write $P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(S^3)$ for the singular complex of \[ \operatorname{Homeo}(S^3\times I\ \mathrm{rel}\ S^3\times\{0\}). \] The upper boundary is free. Write $P_{\mathrm{PL}}(S^3)$ for the simplicial group of jointly finite PL concordances with the same boundary convention.
