Let $D_1,\ldots,D_c$ be effective ample Cartier divisors, with $1\leq c<r$, whose local equations form a regular sequence, and let $Y=D_1\cap\cdots\cap D_c$. For every locally free $E$, completion along $Y$ gives an isomorphism \[ H^q(X,E)\longrightarrow H^q(\widehat X,\widehat E) \quad(q<r-c) \] and an injection for $q=r-c$. The same result is obtained at every stage of the flag, with $c$ replaced by its length. The qualification ``ample'' cannot be dropped.

Let $P=\mathbb P^r_k$, let $Y\subset P$ be closed, and let $0<n<r$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $H^0(P,\mathcal O_P(a))\to H^0(\widehat P,\mathcal O_{\widehat P}(a))$ is an isomorphism and $H^q(\widehat P,\mathcal O_{\widehat P}(a))=0$ for $0<q<n$, for all sufficiently large $a$; \item the same assertions hold for every integer $a$; \item $\operatorname{cd}(P\setminus Y)\leq r-n-1$. \end{enumerate} Replacing $\mathcal O_P(a)$ by $\omega_P(a)$ gives the same criterion. Thus the written $r-n$ on scan 008 is the first vanishing degree, not the usual cohomological dimension. The bound is attained by $Y=\mathbb P^n\subset\mathbb P^r$. For a general pure Cohen--Macaulay projective $X$ of dimension $r$ and $\dim Y\leq n$, the diagonal margin on scan 003 has the correct comparison \[ H^q(X,E)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(X\setminus Y,E) \quad(q<r-n-1) \tag{C.19.1} \] for locally free $E$, including $q=0$ when $n<r-1$. The further claim that these groups vanish for $0<q<r-n-1$ needs vanishing on $X$ itself and is false for general such $X$.

Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a complete noetherian local Cohen--Macaulay ring of dimension $r$, with canonical module $\omega_A$. Put $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $a=V(\mathfrak m)$, $U=X\setminus\{a\}$, and let $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$, $Y=V(I)$ and $Y'=Y\cap U$. Let $P$ be a bounded complex with finite cohomology modules on $X$ and put $Q=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,\omega_A)$. For the injective hull $E_A$ of the residue field, write $\mathbb D=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(-,E_A)$. Completion with a hat below is along $Y$, not along a newly chosen closed point. There are natural isomorphisms \begin{align} \mathbb D P&\simeq R\Gamma_a(X,Q)[r],& \mathbb D R\Gamma_a(X,P)&\simeq Q[r],\tag{C.21.1}\\ \mathbb D R\Gamma(U,P)&\simeq R\Gamma(U,Q)[r-1],\tag{C.21.2}\\ \mathbb D R\Gamma_Y(X,P)&\simeq R\Gamma_a(\widehat X,\widehat Q)[r],\tag{C.21.3}\\ \mathbb D R\Gamma_{Y'}(U,P)&\simeq R\Gamma(\widehat U,\widehat Q)[r-1].\tag{C.21.4} \end{align} They identify the dual of \[ R\Gamma_a(X,P)\longrightarrow R\Gamma_Y(X,P) \longrightarrow R\Gamma_{Y'}(U,P)\longrightarrow \tag{C.21.5} \] with the formal localization triangle, with its arrows reversed and the displayed shifts. In particular, for perfect $F$ and bounded coherent $G$, take $P=R\mathcal Hom(F,G)$ and $Q=R\mathcal Hom(G,F\otimes^L\omega_A)$. When $A$ is Gorenstein and a trivialization $\omega_A\simeq A$ is chosen, these are exactly the swapped-argument Ext groups drawn on scan 006, with $X'=U$ and subscript $a$ denoting support at the closed point. The $r-1$ is forced by localization. More generally, for closed $Y\subseteq Z\subseteq X$ containing $a$, the dual of the localization triangle $R\Gamma_Y P\to R\Gamma_Z P\to R\Gamma_{Z\setminus Y}(X\setminus Y,P)$ is the triangle determined by the restriction \[ R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Z,\widehat Q_Z) \longrightarrow R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Y,\widehat Q_Y). \tag{C.21.6} \] Precisely, the dual of the relative term is \[ \mathbb D R\Gamma_{Z\setminus Y}(X\setminus Y,P) \simeq \operatorname{Cone}\bigl( R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Z,\widehat Q_Z)\to R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Y,\widehat Q_Y)\bigr)[r-1]. \] Iteration proves the same assertion for every successive difference of a finite closed filtration, including all endpoint connecting maps. This is the complete localization induction visible in the last two rows of the page.

Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a complete noetherian local ring, put $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}$, and let $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$. Let $F,G$ be finite $A$-modules and write $F_b=(F/I^bF)|_U$. If $\widehat U$ is the formal completion along $V(I)\cap U$, then, for every $q\geq0$, \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_{\widehat U}(\widehat G,\widehat F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_b\operatorname{Ext}^q_U(G|_U,F_b). \tag{C.22.1} \] No regularity, Cohen--Macaulayness or local freeness is required for this inverse-limit statement.

For the seven conditions in C.014, the following attributions follow from the opened primary texts. They distinguish the ambient scheme from the closed subscheme and do not replace a source hypothesis by Cohen--Macaulayness without proof. \begin{enumerate} \item SGA~2, XII, 1.1--1.4, pp.~109--111, supplies projective Serre duality and the equivalence of eventual negative-twist vanishing with depth at closed points. It is not the full complement/formal-completion equivalence for arbitrary $Y$. XII, Theorem~2.1, Corollary~2.2 and Lemma~2.3, pp.~114--115 (original margins 143--144), give comparison for an ample effective section regular on the coherent sheaf, in a projective family, with the stated fibrewise depth and flatness hypotheses. Over a field, depth $>d$ at closed points gives isomorphisms below $d$ and a monomorphism at $d$. In particular, for a pure Cohen--Macaulay $r$-fold, an ample Cartier divisor, and a vector bundle, the bound is $d=r-1$. This is a sufficient geometric hypothesis, not a converse for an arbitrary closed $Y$. The proof and its precise scope are C.018 with $c=1$. \item Hartshorne, \emph{Ample subvarieties of algebraic varieties} (1970), III, Theorem~3.4(b), p.~96, with proof on pp.~97--98, contains both directions of C.014(1)$\Longleftrightarrow$(7) when $X$ is a complete nonsingular variety. If $\dim X=r$ and the cohomological dimension bound is $\operatorname{cd}U\leq a$, its comparison is an isomorphism for $q<r-a-1$ and injective for $q=r-a-1$. Put $a=m-1$ to obtain exactly $q<r-m$ and the boundary injection in C.014. III, Proposition~3.1, p.~92, supplies the negative-twist test in the smooth quasiprojective case; III, Theorem~3.3, pp.~94--96, supplies formal duality. These statements use a nonsingular ambient variety. C.011--C.014 give the argument for a projective Cohen--Macaulay ambient scheme whose canonical module need not be invertible. \item Hartshorne, \emph{Cohomology of non-complete algebraic varieties} (1971), Proposition~2.9, p.~261, assumes $X=\mathbb P^r_k$ and condition $(I_s^*)$: for $i<s$, $\bigoplus_{v\in\mathbb Z}H^i(\widehat X, \mathcal O_{\widehat X}(v))$ is a finite free graded $k[x_0,\ldots,x_r]$-module generated in degree zero. For an integer $d\leq s$, the proposition gives both directions between $\operatorname{cd}U<r-d$, vanishing in those degrees for the single untwisted sheaf $\omega_X$, and the isomorphisms $H^q(X,\mathcal O_X)\to H^q(\widehat X, \mathcal O_{\widehat X})$ for $q<d$. It does not state an additional boundary injection. For the range $0<d<r$ considered here that injection for $\mathcal O_X$ is automatic, since $H^d(\mathbb P^r, \mathcal O)=0$; it is not a substitute for the vector-bundle boundary condition of C.014(7). Theorem~2.1, p.~259, proves $(I_s^*)$ when $Y$ is purely $s$-dimensional and smooth over a characteristic-zero field, or Cohen--Macaulay over a field of positive characteristic. Here Cohen--Macaulayness is a condition on $Y$, while the ambient scheme remains projective space. Proposition~2.2, p.~260, separately contains an injection at its boundary degree $s-\operatorname{hd}(F)$ for the comparison map constructed there. Let $S$ have six elements. A duad is a two-element subset, a syntheme a partition into three duads, and a total a partition of all fifteen duads into five synthemes. Let $S^*$ be the set of totals. Then $|S^*|=6$, the natural homomorphism $\mathfrak S(S)\longrightarrow\mathfrak S(S^*)$ is an outer isomorphism, and $S\longrightarrow S^{**}$ is a canonical bijection. The duality interchanges duads and synthemes, and gives a canonical bijection between the ten unordered $3+3$ partitions on either side. For each $s\in S$, $t\in S^*$ there is a unique $\operatorname{Stab}(s,t)$-equivariant bijection $S\setminus\{s\}\longrightarrow S^*\setminus\{t\}$. Here is an explicit completion of the undefined marginal term ``bihexagones'' on 119/155. A hexagon is a Hamiltonian cycle in $K_S$, and a bihexagon is a pair of edge-disjoint hexagons. The graph whose vertices are hexagons and whose edges are bihexagons has six connected components, each a Petersen graph. Its components are canonically $S^*$. Thus the duality can indeed be constructed from bihexagons. This supplies a precise construction; the one-word margin does not specify a unique historical definition of that word.

For $S=\{s,c_0,\ldots,c_4\}$, let $F(s;c)$ consist of the five triples $\{s,c_i,c_{i+1}\}$ and the five complements in $\{c_0,\ldots,c_4\}$ of the diagonals $\{c_i,c_{i+2}\}$, with indices modulo five. Complementation inside $\binom S3$ pairs them into six biicosahedral structures. Their automorphism groups are respectively the transitive $\mathfrak A_5$ and $\mathfrak S_5$ in $\mathfrak S_6$. The geometric complex is the antipodal quotient of an ordinary icosahedron, usually called a hemiicosahedron; the adjective ``gauche'' is interpreted in this precise six-vertex sense.

An icosahedron with a vertex is a pentagon on the other five points; a biicosahedron with a vertex is a complementary pair of pentagons. A biicosahedron with a distinguished edge $\varepsilon=\{a,b\}$ is exactly a square $Q$ on the other four vertices, together with an identification $\varepsilon\simeq\operatorname{rot}(Q)$. Choosing one of its two icosahedra is choosing one of the two diagonals of $Q$. An icosahedron with a distinguished face is exactly an ordered pair of three-element sets with a bijection between them. A biicosahedron with a distinguished biface is the corresponding unordered prism. The stabilizers are respectively $D_{10},\operatorname{AGL}_1(5)$, $D_8$, $\mathfrak S_3$, and $\mathfrak S_3\times C_2$.

A set of nine points carrying twelve three-element blocks, any two \emph{distinct} blocks meeting in at most one point, is the affine plane $\mathbb F_3^2$, uniquely up to isomorphism. Condition c) alone does not imply nine blocks, even if every block has four elements.

Let $V=\mathbb F_3^2$, let $E$ be its twelve lines, and let $I$ be its four directions. Consider an oriented disc $D$, a finite union $K$ of disjoint properly embedded arcs with distinct endpoints on $\partial D$, a nonempty $n$-element set $S\subset\partial D\setminus K$, and a root $s_0\in S$. Every component of $\partial D\setminus\partial K$ must contain at least one mark, and every such component outside the region containing $s_0$ must contain exactly one. These are the data and conditions on 003. Their isotopy groupoid is equivalent to the following explicit groupoid of word types: a rooted cyclically ordered $n$-set of marks, together with a partial pairing of its $n$ gaps, noncrossing, such that after cutting at the root no pair encloses an unpaired gap. Morphisms preserve the root, cyclic order, and pairing. Equivalently a type can be written as a linear word of $n$ positions with a specified cancellation matching: paired letters are the two occurrences of a private symbol with opposite exponents; every unpaired letter has its own private symbol; the pairing is noncrossing and encloses no unpaired letter. Renaming symbols and reversing the chosen name of a paired symbol changes no type. Unspecified equality patterns of ordinary free-group words are not the object classified by the page. Under the reading ``isotypique'' as a set of isomorphism types, take isomorphism classes of these same finite data. Under the reading ``isotopique'', retain their combinatorial isomorphisms, which are exactly the isotopy classes of homeomorphisms. If orientation is forgotten, allow order reversal; its possible reflection automorphisms must be retained for a groupoid equivalence. Neither reading identifies the raw groupoid of all homeomorphisms with a finite combinatorial groupoid.

An involution on a linearly ordered finite set is reducible to the identity by repeatedly deleting \emph{both} members of an adjacent two-cycle if and only if its two-cycles do not interlace and no two-cycle encloses a fixed point. For a fixed-point-free involution this is exactly noncrossing. Deleting only one member and making the survivor fixed, as a literal completion of 152/004's one-edge contraction, fails already for $(1\ 4)(2\ 3)$.

A finite oriented combinatorial map without isolated vertices is a finite dart set $D$, a fixed-point-free involution $\alpha$ pairing its darts into edges, and a permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles are the cyclically ordered vertices. Its boundary permutation is $\tau=\sigma\alpha$; its faces are the cycles of $\tau$. Connectedness is transitivity of $\langle\sigma,\alpha\rangle$. Conversely these permutations reconstruct the oriented ribbon neighbourhood and, after capping its boundary components, the closed oriented surface, uniquely up to oriented homeomorphism. With one face, $|D|=2m$ and $c(\pi)$ denoting number of cycles, \[ g=\frac{m+1-c(\tau\alpha)}2. \] The following are equivalent: the graph is a tree; $g=0$; its boundary pairing is noncrossing. This is exactly the corrected content of 152/010--013. The point tree is an additional zero-dart object.

The dictionary of E.012 is the ordinary oriented map dictionary. Subdividing each edge by a white midpoint makes the original vertices black and turns the map into a clean dessin: every white vertex has degree two. On the same dart set its permutations are \[ \sigma_0=\sigma,\qquad\sigma_1=\alpha, \qquad\sigma_\infty=(\sigma\alpha)^{-1}, \qquad\sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_\infty=1. \] Plane trees are precisely its connected genus-zero one-face instances. The passage in the Esquisse to algebraic curves and Galois action is additional arithmetic structure on this same combinatorial category, not a different boundary-pairing criterion.

All the configurations above have explicit geometric realizations over their indicated fields. An $n$-cube with labelled coordinate directions is a product $\prod_{i\in I}P_i$ of two-element coordinate torsors; its dual cross-polytope has vertices $\coprod_iP_i$. Its orientation torsor is $\omega(I)\wedge\bigwedge_iP_i$, and its antipodal map has sign $(-1)^n$. For $n=3$, a cube is equivalently its four body diagonals and its orientation torsor, with automorphism group $\mathfrak S_4\times C_2$. The affine and projective planes in E.007 are realized over $\mathbb F_3$; they cannot be realized faithfully by nine distinct real points and straight lines with exactly the affine-plane incidences. The anharmonic ratios in 119/160 are the usual six transforms \[ \lambda,\quad1-\lambda,\quad\lambda^{-1},\quad (1-\lambda)^{-1},\quad\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda},\quad \frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}. \] On $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_3)$ they all equal $-1$. On $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_4)$ an ordering of its five points gives an orientation precisely by choosing one of the two values in $\mathbb F_4\setminus\mathbb F_2$, as stated on the page.

\label{SA21-A02} $\Sigma(E)$ is a complete ortholattice, with \[ \bigwedge_i A_i=\bigcap_i A_i,\qquad \bigvee_i A_i=\operatorname{cl}\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr),\qquad A^\perp=N(A),\quad 0=\varnothing,\quad1=E. \] For $E=\varnothing$ this is the one-element ortholattice, with $0=1$.

\label{SA21-A03} Let $E$ be an arbitrary orthoset. Its support lattice is orthomodular if and only if \begin{equation}\label{eq:basis-test} \text{for every }S\subseteq E\text{ and every basis }D\subseteq N(S), \qquad N(D)\subseteq N(N(S)). \end{equation} In particular, the exact answer for the comparability disjoncteur of a poset $L$ is the following condition expressed entirely in its order: for every $S\subseteq L$ and every maximal chain $D$ of $N_L(S)$, every point strictly comparable with all of $D$ is strictly comparable with every point of $N_L(S)$.

\label{SA21-A04} For any orthoset $E$, finite or infinite, $\Sigma(E)$ is Boolean if and only if \begin{equation}\label{eq:boolean-test} x\not\perp y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\exists z\in E)\ N(x)\cup N(y)\subseteq N(z). \end{equation} The quantifier includes $x=y$. For a comparability disjoncteur this is the required necessary and sufficient condition on the order of $L$, using $N_L$ in place of $N$. For finite $L$, it is a direct test on triples of points and their neighbourhoods; no lattice enumeration is required.

\label{SA21-A06} The lattice $\Sigma(M(L))$ is orthomodular exactly when the order test of Theorem~\ref{SA21-A03} holds on the explicit positional poset in Definition~\ref{SA21-A05}. Equivalently, for every set $S$ of points and intervals and every maximal positional chain $D$ of those symbols strictly comparable with all of $S$, \[ N_{M(L)}(D)\subseteq N_{M(L)}(N_{M(L)}(S)). \] It is Boolean exactly when the nonisolated points of $L$ form a chain. Here a point is nonisolated if it is comparable with a distinct point of $L$; all remaining points may be arbitrary isolated points. For a nontrivial connected $L$, the Boolean condition is simply that $L$ is a chain. No finiteness or local finiteness is assumed.

\label{SA21-A07} Let $L=\{a,b,c,d\}$ with exactly $a<c,a<d,b<c,b<d$. Then $M(L)$ has eight strata. Its edges are the four point edges \[ ac,ad,bc,bd \] and the two endpoint edges for each of $I_{ac},I_{ad},I_{bc},I_{bd}$. Its twenty supports are: $\varnothing$; the eight singleton sets; the six two-element subsets of $\{P_a,P_b,P_c,P_d\}$; the four neighbourhoods $N(P_x)$; and $M(L)$. The strict inclusion \[ A=\{P_a\}<B=\{P_a,P_b\},\qquad B\cap A^\perp=\varnothing \] violates orthomodularity. Nevertheless every figure satisfies Axiome supp~1, and the graph satisfies Sumner's Dacey-graph condition. Taking the positional order itself as an eight-element poset also refutes L2 for comparability disjoncteurs.

\label{SA21-A08} For an orthoset in which all cliques are admitted as figures, the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item For every clique $F$ and $A\subseteq F$, $\operatorname{cl}F\cap N(A)=\operatorname{cl}(F\setminus A)$. \item For every maximal clique $D$ and every distinct $u,v$, $D\subseteq N(u)\cup N(v)$ implies $u\perp v$. \end{enumerate} The equivalence holds also for infinite cliques, using choice. On finite graphs (2) is precisely \citet[p.~492]{Sumner1974}, and is normality in the terminology of \citet[Definition 2.4 and Lemma 2.5] {PasekaVetterlein2022}. On an infinite orthoset their normality tests finite orthogonal families; we do not identify that convention with an unrestricted infinite-family assertion. The finite condition is strictly weaker than the basis criterion of Theorem~\ref{SA21-A03}, even for finite comparability graphs.

\label{SA21-A09} Every finite prefigure, and hence every finite figure, of $M(L)$ satisfies Axiome supp~1 for every poset $L$. This conclusion does not assert orthomodularity of the whole support lattice, nor does it extend to arbitrary infinite figures.

\label{SA21-A10} Let $L=\mathbb Q\amalg\{a,b\}$, with the usual order on $\mathbb Q$, with $a<q$ exactly for $q\geq0$, and with $q<b$ exactly for $q<0$. There are no other comparisons involving $a,b$. The countable figure $F=\{P_q:q\in\mathbb Q\}$ of $M(L)$ violates Axiome supp~1. Thus a statement for finite flags cannot silently be upgraded to all figures of the maximal, infinitary magasin.

\label{SA21-A11} Put $I=\{i,i',j,k\}$ and let \[ \mathcal T=\{E\subseteq I:(i\in E\Longleftrightarrow i'\in E)\} \cup\{\{i\},\{i',j,k\}\}. \] Ordered by inclusion, with orthocomplement $E\mapsto I\setminus E$, $\mathcal T$ is a ten-element ortholattice and is not orthomodular. It reconstructs the set formula of 156-9, scan 113. We assign \[ \begin{array}{c|cccccccccc} \text{label}&0&a'&a&b&c&A&A'&B&C&1\\ \hline \text{set}&\varnothing&\{i\}&\{i,i'\}&\{j\}&\{k\}& \{j,k\}&\{i',j,k\}&\{i,i',k\}&\{i,i',j\}&I \end{array} \] The covers are \[ 0\prec a'\prec a,\quad0\prec b,\quad0\prec c,\quad a\prec B,C,\quad b\prec A,C,\quad c\prec A,B,\quad A\prec A'\prec1,\quad B,C\prec1. \] In particular, a transcribed edge $c\to C$ must not be included.

\label{SA21-A12} Let $(M,\rho,\perp)$ be a magasin whose interior refinement $\rho$ is a preorder and whose faithfulness means \[ x\perp y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{there is no }z\text{ with }z\rho x\text{ and }z\rho y. \] In the Alexandrov topology of $\rho$-lower sets, $\Sigma(M)$ is exactly the complete Boolean algebra of regular open sets. In particular every family of mutually orthogonal supports satisfies the relative-complement and nonempty-meet conclusions of the support theorem.

\label{SA21-A13} Assume the strong Mag~1--4, divisibility, and the lieu-detection axiom Mag~L2. Let $L$ be the set of lieux and $U_X=\{p\in L:p\rho X\}$. In this notation Mag~L2 says \[ X\perp Y\iff U_X\perp U_Y. \] The maps \[ \Sigma(M)\longrightarrow\Sigma(L),\ S\longmapsto S\cap L, \qquad \Sigma(L)\longrightarrow\Sigma(M),\ T\longmapsto\widehat T=\{X:U_X\subseteq T\} \] are inverse complete ortholattice isomorphisms. Thus the exact class asked for in A.2 consists of those magasins whose lieu graph satisfies \eqref{eq:basis-test}. Their Boolean subclass is given exactly by \eqref{eq:boolean-test} on that graph. Every orthoset occurs as the lieu graph of a magasin satisfying these hypotheses.

\label{SA21-A14} In any atelier with the specified orthogonality relation, the nonzero support $\operatorname{cl}\{x\}$ of a lieu $x$ is an atom if and only if \begin{equation}\label{eq:atom-test} N(x)\subseteq N(y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N(x)=N(y) \qquad (y\in M). \end{equation} Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{SA21-A13}, it suffices to test $y\in L$. Hence the exact class in A.3 is given by \eqref{eq:atom-test} for every lieu. The stronger assertion that $\operatorname{cl}\{x\}=\{x\}$ requires $N(x)\subseteq N(y)\Rightarrow y=x$ and is different.

\label{SA21-A15} Two lieux with no edge have the two-element Boolean support lattice; their supports are the same atom. Thus nondisjoint distinct lieux do not, by themselves, measure failure of distributivity. Under Mag~L2 and divisibility, the following are equivalent: faithfulness; Booleanity with lieux represented by distinct atoms; and $p\perp q$ for every pair of distinct lieux. In the additional point-separating case $\operatorname{cl}\{p\}=\{p\}$ for all lieux, Booleanity alone is equivalent to pairwise disjointness of distinct lieux. Without point separation the exact replacement is Theorem~\ref{SA21-A04}. For interval magasins the exact replacement is the nonisolated-core criterion of Theorem~\ref{SA21-A06}. In particular, for a connected poset $L$, Booleanity of $\Sigma_{M(L)}$ is equivalent to totality of $L$, hence to disjointness of distinct lieux. Thus this precise connected interpretation of the qualitative claim in L3 is true. The unqualified claim fails even in a divisible interval magasin with genuine interval strata: take $L=\mathbb Q\amalg\{c\}$, with $c$ incomparable to every rational.

\label{SA21-A16} Fix an orthoset $E$ and a family $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ of nonempty mutually orthogonal subsets. Put $e_i=\operatorname{cl}U_i$, $S_A=\operatorname{cl}(\bigcup_{i\in A}U_i)$ for $A\subseteq I$, and $S=S_I$. The map $A\mapsto S_A$ is always an injective order map preserving arbitrary joins. The following explicit condition is necessary and sufficient for the remaining lattice conclusions (a)--(c) of the Théorème of 156-7, scan 94: \begin{equation}\label{eq:figure-test} \begin{gathered} z\in S,\quad w\in E,\quad (\forall i\in I)\ [z\perp U_i\ \text{or}\ w\perp U_i] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z\perp w. \end{gathered} \end{equation} More precisely this is equivalent to all identities \[ S_A\cap N\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in B}U_i\Bigr)=S_{A\setminus B} \qquad(B\subseteq A\subseteq I), \] and it implies preservation of arbitrary nonempty meets. Empty meets are preserved into the interval $[0,S]$; they are preserved into the whole lattice only when $S=1$. For the atelier specialization take $I=\widetilde F$ for an admitted figure $F$, and $E=M$ with the \emph{old whole-figure disjunction} $\parallel$, and write $N_\parallel$ for its polar. Here $U_X$ are the actual open-stratum subsets used to define $S_A$, or subsets with the same polars as justified below. For every incidence-closed subfigure $G\leq F$, clause (d) has the additional exact criterion \begin{equation}\label{eq:incidence-coverage} N_\parallel(\widetilde G) =N_\parallel\Bigl(\bigcup_{X\in\widetilde G}U_X\Bigr). \end{equation} Here $\operatorname{Supp}(G)=N_\parallel^2(\widetilde G)$. Under the older hypotheses of scan 94, nonemptiness, mutual orthogonality and \eqref{eq:incidence-coverage} are automatic; the exact class asked for in A.4 is then given by \eqref{eq:figure-test} for every admitted figure. If those hypotheses are dropped, include all three of these requirements explicitly. Injectivity forces nonemptiness, and the relative-complement formula for two different indices forces orthogonality. This formulation applies to infinite figures and infinite families.

\label{SA21-A17} In a complete orthomodular lattice, every mutually orthogonal family of nonzero elements satisfies the lattice clauses (a)--(c) of Theorem~\ref{SA21-A16}. Conversely, if the relative-complement formula holds for every two-element orthogonal family of nonzero lattice elements, the lattice is orthomodular. Thus 156-9, scan 117, applied to the universal spatial figures of a spatios, is equivalent to orthomodularity. The axiom for the actual figures of a given magasin is weaker, even under Mag~1--4, divisibility and Mag~L2.

\label{SA21-A18} Take four lieux $a',a,b,b'$ with identity incidence and interior refinement and only the edges $a'a,ab,bb'$. Then every strong Mag axiom, divisibility and Mag~L2 hold, but Axiome supp~1 fails for $F=\{a,b\}$: \[ \operatorname{cl}F=E,\qquad \operatorname{cl}F\cap N(a)=\{a',b\}\ne\{b\} =\operatorname{cl}\{b\}. \] Its support lattice is $O_6$. If ``disjunctive'' is given the stronger spatial interpretation in which interior refinement is reconstructed from supports, use instead the five-cycle with identity incidence and interior refinement: its singleton supports are singletons, so that reconstruction is identity, and the same axiom fails. Thus both readings of the request after the marginal ``Oui!'' of 156-8, scan 89, have an explicit counterexample.

\label{SA21-A19} The five-cycle with identity incidence and refinement is an atelier satisfying the older At~1--7, At~L1--L3, CL(spac), At~D, At~supp and the old absorption axiom At~supp~1 of 156-7, scan 87. Nevertheless the relative-complement conclusion of scan 94 fails, so the theorem as a whole is false under its stated hypotheses.

\label{SA21-A20} Let $M=\{a,b\}$, with identity incidence, interior refinement $a\rho b$ in addition to identities, and no internal disjunction. The figures are $\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\}$. Let $P=\{p,q\}$ and define the external support function \[ |a|=\{p\},\qquad |b|=\{p,q\}. \] It is faithful and normalized, but not fully faithful in the exact sense of 156-8, scan 86.

\label{SA21-A21} A spatios satisfying Spat~1--3 of 156-9, scans 51--53 and 78--80, is exactly a complete ortholattice. For a complete ortholattice $K$, put $E_K=K\setminus\{0\}$ and $x\perp y\iff x\leq y^\perp$. Then \[ K\longrightarrow\Sigma(E_K),\quad s\longmapsto\{x\ne0:x\leq s\} \] is a complete ortholattice isomorphism. If zero is retained, the relation is not irreflexive; the manuscript allows a self-orthogonal point only when it is orthogonal to every point. Removing this radical is the exact comparison with ordinary orthosets.

\label{SA21-A22} Let $E,F$ be orthosets. A saturated correspondence of the final 156-9 construction is a map $\alpha:E\to\Sigma(F)$ such that \begin{equation}\label{eq:bond} x\in\operatorname{cl}_E A\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha(x)\subseteq\bigvee_{a\in A}\alpha(a) \qquad(A\subseteq E). \end{equation} It corresponds bijectively to a complete join-preserving map $f:\Sigma(E)\to\Sigma(F)$ by \[ f(S)=\bigvee_{x\in S}\alpha(x),\qquad \alpha(x)=f(\operatorname{cl}_E\{x\}). \] Composition is $(\beta\alpha)(x)=\bigvee_{y\in\alpha(x)}\beta(y)$ and the identity is $x\mapsto\operatorname{cl}\{x\}$. If $g$ is the order right adjoint of $f$, the transposed correspondence induces $f^\dagger=C_EgC_F$, characterized by \[ f(S)\perp T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\perp f^\dagger(T). \] Consequently orthosets with these correspondences are equivalent as a category to complete ortholattices with all complete join maps. They are not the category of orthosets with ordinary functions preserving orthogonality. L7 is false with that unqualified morphism claim and true only with this explicit object and arrow dictionary.

\label{SA21-A23} Let $(E,\preceq,\perp)$ have a partial incidence order and an orthoset relation. For each $x$ label its principal incidence ideal by $y\mapsto\operatorname{cl}\{y\}$, transporting the incidence order. Assume that these labels form an elementary ordered spatial figure: the labels are nonzero, distinct, and pairwise orthogonal. Assume also that the resulting ordered deployment $D_x$ determines $x$ injectively. There is then a unique spatial interior refinement making these data a strong magasin. It is given by the existence of an order-preserving carrier \[ h:D_x\longrightarrow D_y,\qquad S\subseteq h(S), \qquad h(\operatorname{cl}\{x\})=\operatorname{cl}\{y\}. \] This is the fully typed interpretation of At~spat~1--3 in 156-9, scan 50, using the spatial target explicitly defined on scan 48. If that target is read merely as disjoint subsets of $E$, the assertion is false and strong At~4 must be added.

\label{SA21-A24} The supplied eight-stratum example satisfies its stated older hypotheses, and both nonempty-meet preservation and relative complementation fail in one figure. Its complete data are \[ M=\{a,b,X,p,e,w,h,g\},\qquad a,b\lhd X,\quad p\rho X, \] with no other nonidentity generating incidences or interior refinements. The lieu graph on $\{a,b,p,e,w,h,g\}$ has edges \[ ab,ap,bp,ae,bw,pw,eh,hg,gw. \] Internal disjunction adds $Xa,Xb,Xw$. Old full figure-disjointness has the displayed lieu edges and no edge at $X$.
\label{SA21-A25} Every finite cograph has an orthomodular support lattice. The converse fails even for a five-element comparability poset with a Boolean support lattice.

\label{SA21-A05a} For every poset $L$, the relations of Definition~\ref{SA21-A05} satisfy strong Mag~1--4. The magasin $M(L)$ is faithful if and only if $L$ is a chain, including the empty and one-point cases. In the full atlas its figures are precisely the positional chains closed under adjoining interval endpoints. Restricting the atlas to finite figures gives exactly the finite such chains; no local finiteness or density of $L$ is needed.

\label{SA21-A14a} For every poset $L$, the lieux of $M(L)$ are exactly the point symbols $P_x$. All these lieux have atomic supports if and only if $L$ is an antichain or $L$ has no isolated points. Thus every lieu has an atomic support for every nonempty connected poset, including the singleton. For $L=\varnothing$ the assertion is vacuous.

\label{SA21-A26} For an arbitrary poset $L$, let $S(L)=L\times\{-,+\}$ with $x^-<x^+$ and $x^\epsilon<y^\delta$ whenever $x<y$ in $L$. The maps \[ P_x\longmapsto[x^-<x^+],\qquad I_{a,b}\longmapsto[a^+<b^-]\quad(a<b) \] embed the disjoncteur of $M(L)$ as an induced subspace $U$ of $Q^+(S(L))$. They induce an isomorphism of complete ortholattices \[ \Sigma_{M(L)}\cong\mathcal C\bigl(Q^+(S(L))\bigr). \] The isomorphism and its inverse are given explicitly by trace and by the finite-piece extension described in the proof. No finiteness, boundedness, connectedness or existence of meets and joins is assumed.
\label{SA21-A27a} If $P$ is a finite conditional lattice, then $\mathcal C(Q^+(P))$ is orthomodular.

\label{SA21-A27} For every finite poset $L$, \[ \Sigma_{M(L)}\text{ is orthomodular} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\text{ is a conditional lattice}. \] The conclusion does not require $L$ to be bounded or connected.

\label{SA21-B-prime-representation} Suppose every bounded family in the nonempty poset \(\mathscr F\) has a join, and every figure is the join of its completely join-irreducible strata. Then \(F\mapsto\widetilde F\) is an order embedding and preserves all nonempty meets. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item it preserves every bounded join as a union; \item all strata satisfy \textup{(B.P)}; \item its image contains every downward-closed subset of every one of its members, with joins there given by unions. \end{enumerate} Under these equivalent conditions, compatibility by strata is precisely the condition that two admitted downsets have an admitted union whenever all their cross-pairs of principal ideals have admitted unions. If every figure has finitely many strata, the prime condition is equivalent to distributivity of every principal figure ideal.

\label{SA21-B-M3} Let \(\mathscr F=M_3=\{0,a,b,c,1\}\), with three incomparable atoms and \(a\vee b=a\vee c=b\vee c=1\). Put \(\ll=\leq\). All bounded joins exist; the completely join-irreducibles are \(a,b,c\); every figure is their join; all pairs are compatible. Thus literal C1--C3 hold. Refinement by strata holds because deployment inclusion detects the order. The carrier of an atom in any figure containing it is that atom; compatibility plus refinement implies incidence; internal refinement on \(M\) is equality. Thus the displayed At 1--At 7 clauses also hold when \(M\) is defined by the equality-based irreducibility of 156-4 and 156-8. Nevertheless \[ \widetilde{a\vee b}=\{a,b,c\}\ne\{a,b\} =\widetilde a\cup\widetilde b. \] The downset \(\{a,b\}\) of \(\widetilde1\) is not a deployment. This example survives the literal atlas axioms of 156-8, scans 20--21. On \(M=\{a,b,c\}\), take incidence and refinement to be equality and \(x\delta y\) to mean \(x\ne y\). Mag 1--4 hold: all principal deployments are singletons, and internal heredity is trivial. Atlas At 1 is bounded completeness, At 2 is generation, At 3 is total compatibility, At 4 is the deployment test for refinement, and At 5(a) is satisfied by defining \(\delta\) only on elementary objects. At 5(b) holds because distinct atoms are \(\delta\)-related. Thus \emph{even atlas At 1--5 plus Mag 1--4 does not imply the advertised downset representation}. Adding (B.P) is necessary and sufficient.

\label{SA21-B-preliminary-admissibility} The preliminary set-theoretic Cont 2 at 156-4/27 requires nonempty residuals and binary-intersection coverage; for infinite families these do not imply the later admissibility definition. On \(L=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\), put \(A_n=\{\infty\}\cup\{m\in\mathbb N:m\geq n\}\). The family \(\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) has \(A_n^\circ=\{n\}\) and \(A_n\cap A_m=A_{\max(n,m)}\), but \(\infty\) belongs to no residual and has no least stratum. Adding coverage by the residuals is necessary and sufficient: binary-intersection coverage makes any minimal containing stratum least. The later text explicitly adds that coverage condition \citep[156-5, scans 2--5]{Grothendieck1986}, \path{J156-5-01_transcription.tex:22--37,151--154}. All uses of \(\operatorname{Fig}(L)\) below use this later definition.

\label{SA21-B-carrier-calculus} In a prime atelier with At 4--At 7, carriers compose. If \(P\ll F\) and \(G\leq F\), the displayed formula for \(P|G\) is a figure and is \(\inf_{\ll}(P,G)\). Restrictions commute with incidence unions and with incidence intersections inside a fixed parent. If \(F,G\) are compatible, every common refinement refines \(F\cap G\). These conclusions require no lieux and no finite-dimension hypothesis.

\label{SA21-B-optional-implications} Over the prime core the following implications hold, with exactly the indicated hypotheses: \begin{gather*} \mathrm C\Longrightarrow\mathrm D\Longrightarrow\mathrm D_0, \qquad \mathrm D\Longrightarrow\mathrm L3, \qquad \mathrm C\Longrightarrow\mathrm{At}\,11',\\ \mathrm L2\Longrightarrow\mathrm D_0, \qquad \mathrm L2+\mathrm L3\Longrightarrow\mathrm D, \qquad \mathrm L3+\mathrm{CL(spac)}\Longrightarrow\mathrm C,\\ \mathrm D_0+\mathrm L1+\mathrm{CL(spac)}\Longrightarrow\mathrm L2, \qquad \mathrm D_0+\mathrm L1+\mathrm{CL(pol)}\Longrightarrow\mathrm L2,\\ \mathrm L2+\mathrm{CL(spac)} \Longleftrightarrow\mathrm L2+\mathrm{CD2}, \qquad \mathrm L2+\mathrm{CL(pol)} \Longleftrightarrow\mathrm L2+\mathrm{CD2}' . \end{gather*} At \(11'\) is equivalent to finite-cover gluing. Infinite-cover gluing requires a union-closure hypothesis; At Fil is sufficient. Full canonical figure families have that closure automatically.

\label{SA21-B-mag-equivalence} The following two structures are equivalent, by mutually inverse definitions on the same set \(M\). \begin{enumerate} \item Mag 1--4: \(\leq,\ll\) are partial orders, \(\leq\subseteq\ll\); every nonempty \(\{Z\leq Y:X\ll Z\}\) has a least element; \(\delta\) is symmetric, irreflexive and hereditary under the resulting \(\rho\); and \[ Y,Z\leq X,\ Y\ne Z\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y\delta Z. \tag{B.M4} \] \item The corrected strong Mag \(1'\)--\(4'\): \(\leq,\rho\) are partial orders; \(\delta\) is symmetric and irreflexive; there is at most one \(Z\) with \(X\rho Z\leq Y\); the exchange condition \[ X'\leq X\rho Y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists Y'\leq Y\ (X'\rho Y') \tag{B.E} \] holds; \(\delta\) is hereditary under \(\rho\); and (B.M4) holds. \end{enumerate} The inverse definition is \(X\ll Y\Longleftrightarrow\exists Z\ (X\rho Z\leq Y)\). For either structure define \[ X\bowtie Y\Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\forall A\in\widetilde X\setminus\widetilde Y, B\in\widetilde Y\setminus\widetilde X\bigr)\ A\delta B. \tag{B.MC} \] Every principal downset is a clique. The full family of clique downsets, or any atlas containing all principal downsets and closed under subfigures and finite compatible unions, is a prime atelier with At 1--7, C, D, D\(_0\), L3 and finite gluing. For the full family, arbitrary gluing, At 11 bis and At Fil also hold.

\label{SA21-B-local-equivalence} For a strong magasin, Mog L2 is \[ X\delta Y\Longleftrightarrow (\forall p\in U_X,q\in U_Y)\ p\delta q. \tag{B.Loc} \] It implies Mog L1, \(U_X\ne\varnothing\), by irreflexivity. Under the prime incidence convention, strong magasins with (B.Loc) and their chosen atlases are equivalent to prime ateliers satisfying At 1--7, L1, L2, L3 and CL(spac). The inverse definition of \(\delta\) is the right-hand side of (B.Loc). In the earlier formulation using \(\leq,\ll\), Mog 1, Mog 2, Mog L1 and a symmetric irreflexive graph on the lieux, together with the all-pairs div 4 clause, produce a strong magasin by this definition \emph{if and only if the resulting internal refinement is transitive}. It suffices to impose transitivity when the first object is a lieu; under these hypotheses that restricted condition forces full transitivity. In the later \(\leq,\rho\) formulation, the exact repair is to require nonempty \(U_X\) and replace comparable-only div 3 by the all-pairs condition (B.M4) tested on open lieux.

\label{SA21-B-missing-transitivity} Take \(M=\{p,q,z,u,t\}\), incidence generated by \(z<t\), and refinement generated by \[ p\ll z,\quad p\ll u,\quad q\ll u,\quad u\ll t, \qquad z\ll t. \] Put \(p\parallel q\) on the two lieux. The orders contain identity pairs. Least carriers exist in every principal deployment. The open lieu sets are \[ U_p=U_z=\{p\},\quad U_q=U_t=\{q\},\quad U_u=\{p,q\}. \] Thus Mog 1, Mog 2, divisibility, symmetric irreflexive div 3, and the all-pairs div 4 clause all hold: the only nontrivial incidence pair is \(z<t\), with disjoint open lieu sets. But \(p\rho u\rho t\), whereas \(p\not\rho t\), since \(p\ll z<t\). The defined relation has \(p\delta t\) but not \(p\delta u\), violating Mag 3 along \(u\rho t\). This independently verifies the input counterexample SA21-R8-09 and establishes the exact missing condition in Theorem~\ref{SA21-B-local-equivalence}.

\label{SA21-B-weak-primed} For the weak primed list take \(M=\{y,z,t\}\), \(y<t,z<t\), \(\rho=\mathrm{id}\), and \(\delta=\{(y,t),(t,y),(z,t),(t,z)\}\). The two orders, unique factorization, exchange and heredity all hold. Every strict comparable pair is internally disjoint. But \(y,z<t\) are not internally disjoint, so the supposed principal deployment \(\{y,z,t\}\) is not a figure under (B.MC). If the doubtful mark in final Mag \(4'\) is read as a negation, take instead the two-element chain \(a<t\), with \(\rho=\mathrm{id}\) and \(\delta=\varnothing\). The two partial orders, unique factorization, exchange, symmetry, irreflexivity and heredity all hold, as does the negative comparable-pair clause. Strong Mag 4 fails at \(a<t\). Thus this alternative reading does not restore the equivalence; the certificate checks its own full primed hypothesis list. For the later divisible list, including explicit divisibility, take \(M=\{a,b,c,t\}\), incidence \(a<t,b<t\), and internal refinement \(c\rho t\), besides identities. The lieux are \(a,b,c\), with graph edges \(a\parallel c,b\parallel c\), and no edge \(a\parallel b\). Unique factorization and exchange hold; every open-lieu set is a singleton. The comparable div 3 clause holds for \(a<t,b<t\). The derived \(\delta\) has edges \(ac,bc,at,bt\), but not \(ab\). Again the principal deployment of \(t\) is not a figure. These are genuine finite countermodels to the written weakened clauses, not failures of the corrected clauses.

\label{SA21-B-L6-countermodels} All the following strong magasins use the full canonical figure family. Relations not generated by the displayed pairs are absent. \begin{enumerate} \item Let incidence be equality on \(\{p,q,x,y\}\), refinement be generated by \(p\ll x,q\ll y\), and let the sole undirected \(\delta\)-edge be \(pq\). Mag 1--4 and divisibility hold. Nevertheless \(U_x=\{p\},U_y=\{q\}\) are orthogonal while \(x\not\delta y\); L2 and CL(spac) fail. Every class \(\Sigma\) containing the empty poset and the occurring principal posets also fails At \(9_\Sigma\) on \(x,y\). Thus L6 remains false even if its excluded divisibility axiom is supplied. \item Let incidence and refinement both consist of the two chains \(a<x,b<y\). Let \(\delta\) have edges \(ax,by,ab\). Internal refinement is equality, so Mag 1--4 hold. The only lieux below \(x,y\) are respectively \(a,b\), which are disjoint, but \(x,y\) are not disjoint. This is a second direct failure of L2. \item On \(\{a,x,y\}\), let incidence and refinement be \(a<x,a<y\), and let \(\delta\) have just the edges \(ax,ay\). Mag 1--4, L2, L3 and At supp hold. The two shadows of \(x,y\) are both \(\{a\}\), as is the shadow of their common incidence figure. The exterior criterion is empty and hence true, but \(x,y\) are incompatible. Thus CL(spac), CL(pol), CD2 and \(\mathrm{CD2}'\) all fail, even with At supp. For CD2, every nonempty refinement has a nonempty restriction to \(a\); its antecedent is vacuous. \item On \(\{a,b,c,d\}\), take incidence and refinement \(a<b<c\), with \(d\) isolated, and let \(\delta\) have edges \(ab,ac,bc,ad,bd\), omitting \(cd\). Mag 1--4 hold. The seven figures are \[ 0,\ a,\ d,\ a+d,\ a+b,\ a+b+d,\ a+b+c. \] The principal figure \(a\) subdivides \(b\), because their disjoint figures are exactly \(0,d\). The only subdivision of \(c\) is \(c\) itself, whose restriction to \(b\) is \(b\). Therefore this subdivision of a subfigure does not extend: At 14 fails. \end{enumerate} Every pair, triple, figure and refinement in these models is checked by \texttt{core\_models.py}; the proofs of the general magasin construction verify the incidence and figure axioms as well.

\label{SA21-B-gluing-not-L3} Take \(M=\{x,y,q\}\), incidence \(x<y\), refinement \(x\ll y,q\ll y\), and compatibility consisting of equality and the pair \(x,y\). The figures are \(0,\{x\},\{q\},\{x,y\}\). The lieux are \(x,q\), and \(U_y=\{q\}\). The prime core, L1, L2, CL(spac), At supp and D\(_0\) hold. No two nonempty figures are disjoint, so L2 and D\(_0\) have exactly their stated, mostly vacuous content. Every incidence cover of \(\{x,y\}\) contains \(\{x,y\}\) itself; the other nonzero figures are elementary singletons. Consequently all compatible local refinement data glue uniquely. This checks At 11, including arbitrary covers after deleting repetitions. For parents \(x\leq y\), the refinements \(x\ll x\) and \(q\ll y\) restrict respectively to \(x\) and \(0\) on their intersection. Those restrictions are disjoint, while \(x,q\) are not. Thus D and L3 fail, and so does C. The exhaustive code verifies every finite cover and all its refinement assignments. This also shows why CL(spac) alone must not be confused with the relative C axiom.

\label{SA21-B-fil} Let \(M=\{a_n,x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\), with discrete incidence, refinement generated by \(a_n\ll x_n\), and internal disjointness between exactly those pairs having different indices. This is a strong local magasin: the open-lieu set of either member of the \(n\)-th pair is \(\{a_n\}\). A full figure chooses at most one member of each pair. Restrict the atlas to those figures containing only finitely many \(a_n\), allowing arbitrarily many \(x_n\). It contains all principal figures and is closed under subfigures, bounded unions within the atlas and finite compatible unions. It therefore satisfies all the prime core, local and finite-gluing axioms proved above. Let \(F=\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) and \(G_k=\{a_0,\ldots,a_k\}\). These form an increasing family of refinements of \(F\); their restriction to each stratum \(x_n\) is eventually constant. Their union \(\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is omitted, and no admitted figure can bound it. Thus At Fil, At 11 bis and arbitrary gluing fail. For the last assertion use the disjoint cover of \(F\) by the singleton figures \(x_n\), with local refinements \(a_n\). This identifies the exact extra atlas closure needed by the otherwise valid gluing theorem.

\label{SA21-B-extension-Zorn} For the full figure family of a strong magasin satisfying L1 and At supp, subdivision is equivalent to incidence-maximal refinement, and At 14 follows. This assertion uses the usual axiom of choice through Zorn's lemma. It does not give uniqueness in At 14 bis or ter.

\label{SA21-B-Sigma-gate} Assume the prime core and At 10. Let \(\Sigma\) be a replete class of posets containing all occurring principal deployments. Suppose At \(9_\Sigma\) states \[ X\bowtie Y\Longleftrightarrow \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (\forall p\in\ell(X)\setminus\ell(K), q\in\ell(Y)\setminus\ell(K))\ p\parallel q,\\ \widetilde K\in\Sigma, \end{array}\right. \qquad K=X\cap Y. \tag{B.Sigma} \] For compatible parents \(X,Y\), elementary refinements \(X'\ll X,Y'\ll Y\), and compatible restrictions to \(K=X\cap Y\), the exterior-lieu condition in (B.Sigma) for \(X',Y'\) is automatic. Consequently \[ X'\bowtie Y' \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \widetilde{X'\cap Y'}\in\Sigma. \tag{B.Gate} \] Thus At 12 follows exactly when these common-refinement deployments remain in \(\Sigma\). In particular it follows for unrestricted \(\Sigma\). For \(\Sigma\) equal to the empty poset and posets with a greatest element, it follows if elementary refinements restrict to empty or elementary figures on every elementary subfigure.

\label{SA21-B-Sigma-counter} Take the underlying set \(\{a,b,c,p\}\). We use seven elementary admissible families, with point objects denoted by their points: \[ \begin{array}{c|l} a,b,c,p & \{\{a\}\},\{\{b\}\},\{\{c\}\},\{\{p\}\}\\ k & \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b,c\}\}\\ x & \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b,c\},\{a,b,c,p\}\}\\ x' & \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b,p\}\}. \end{array} \] Incidence is closed-subfamily inclusion; refinement is ordinary set-figure refinement. Declare a pair compatible precisely when it is set-theoretically compatible and its common deployment is empty or elementary. The figures are all downward-closed cliques for this compatibility. The complete nontrivial data are \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} Z&\widetilde Z&\{W:W\ll Z\}&\{W:W\rho Z\}\\ \hline a&\{a\}&\{a\}&\{a\}\\ b&\{b\}&\{b\}&\{b\}\\ c&\{c\}&\{c\}&\{c\}\\ p&\{p\}&\{p\}&\{p\}\\ k&\{a,b,k\}&\{a,b,c,k\}&\{c,k\}\\ x&\{a,b,k,x\}&\{a,b,c,p,k,x,x'\}&\{p,x,x'\}\\ x'&\{a,b,x'\}&\{a,b,p,x'\}&\{p,x'\}. \end{array} \] The incompatible distinct pairs are exactly \[ (c,k),(c,x),(p,x),(p,x'),(k,x'),(x,x'). \] There are 21 figures: the sixteen subsets of the four point objects, and \[ \{a,b,k\},\quad\{a,b,k,p\},\quad\{a,b,k,x\},\quad \{a,b,x'\},\quad\{a,b,c,x'\}. \] Take \(\Sigma\) to be the class consisting of the empty poset and all posets having a greatest element. Every principal deployment is a figure. The table gives two partial orders, unique carriers for every stratum refining every figure, coincidence of incidence and refinement on compatible objects, and transitive internal refinement. Thus the prime At 1--7 hold. The lieux are exactly \(a,b,c,p\), and the open lieu sets of \(k,x,x'\) are respectively \(\{c\},\{p\},\{p\}\); hence At 8. Distinct points are disjoint, and ordinary support disjointness is exactly figure disjointness, giving At 9. Compatible distinct objects have disjoint open lieu sets, giving At 10. The explicit compatibility definition is exactly (B.Sigma), so At \(9_\Sigma\) holds. These assertions, including all figure carriers, are exhaustively checked in \texttt{finite\_axioms.py}. Now use compatible parents \(k\leq x\), with refinements \(k\ll k\) and \(x'\ll x\). Their restrictions to \(K=k\) are \(k\) and \(\{a,b\}\), which are compatible. But \(k,x'\) are incompatible: their common deployment \(\{a,b\}\) has two incomparable maximal elements and is not in \(\Sigma\). This refutes the proposed implication. The same program verifies D and the matching-overlap criterion for \emph{every} compatible figure-parent pair and every refining figure pair. Therefore At 11 also holds, by finite gluing. Adding At 11 and At D does not repair the implication.

\label{SA21-B-extension-unique} Let \(M=\{a,x\}\), let incidence be equality, let refinement have \(a\ll x\), and let internal disjointness be empty. The full figures are \(0,a,x\); two nonempty figures are compatible only when equal, and no nonempty figures are disjoint. Mag 1--4 hold: every principal deployment is a singleton, carriers are unique, and all orthogonality clauses are vacuous. The sole lieu is \(a\), and \(U_a=U_x=\{a\}\). Thus Mog L2, the local axioms, the prime core, C, D, all gluing and At supp hold. Every nonempty refinement has the same cosupport, so \(a\preceq x\). Take \(F=x\), \(G=G'=0\). Both choices \(F'=x\) and \(F'=a\) are subdivisions. Their deployment maps are isomorphisms of one-point posets, their restrictions over \(G\) are empty, and the deployment squares are cartesian. The complementary deployment map is an isomorphism. The mixed incidence condition is vacuous. Hence both satisfy At 14 bis, but they are different figures. Their boundaries are both empty, so At 14 ter's uniqueness also fails. This model satisfies At 14 bis \emph{existence for every possible diagram}: the finite certificate enumerates all six extension diagrams and all twelve gluing assignments.

\label{SA21-B-deployment-unique} Fix posets \(\widetilde G\subseteq\widetilde F\), with \(\widetilde G\) a downset, and a monotone map \(r:\widetilde G'\to\widetilde G\). A deployment square with inverse image \(\widetilde G'\), an isomorphism over \(\widetilde F\setminus\widetilde G\), and the intended mixed incidence rule is unique up to unique isomorphism over these data. Its poset is \[ E=\widetilde G'\amalg(\widetilde F\setminus\widetilde G), \] with the original orders on each piece, no exterior-to-interior relations, and \[ \xi\leq\eta\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r(\xi)\leq\eta \qquad(\xi\in\widetilde G',\ \eta\in\widetilde F\setminus\widetilde G). \] This is a uniqueness theorem for an abstract ordered deployment. An atelier can have several objects with this same deployment and carrier map, as Counterexample~\ref{SA21-B-extension-unique} shows. Requiring a coarsest extension is an additional property, not a consequence of the displayed deployment diagram.

\label{SA21-B-Atstar} The groupoid of prime ateliers with At 4--At 7 is equivalent to the groupoid of pairs \((E,\mathscr H\subseteq\operatorname{Fig}(E))\) with the following five properties: \begin{enumerate} \item \(\varnothing\in\mathscr H\), and \(\mathscr H\) is closed under unions bounded by a member of \(\mathscr H\). \item If \(A\in\Phi\cap\Psi\), the principal subfigures \(\Phi_A=\{B\in\Phi:B\subseteq A\}\) and \(\Psi_A\) agree, \emph{and their common value belongs to \(\mathscr H\)}. Denote it by \(\widehat A\). \item For occurring strata \(A\subseteq B\), \(\widehat A\ll\widehat B\) as set-theoretic figures. \item If \(\widehat A\cup\widehat B\in\mathscr H\) for every \(A\in\Phi,B\in\Psi\), then \(\Phi\cup\Psi\in\mathscr H\). \item \(\mathscr U=\bigcup_{\Phi\in\mathscr H}\Phi\) is an admissible family of support \(E\), and it separates the points of \(E\). \end{enumerate} The italicized membership clause is present at scan 32, but omitted from the shortened final At\(^*2\) list at scan 34. With that clause retained, the converse is valid. Without it, if all displayed refinements are interpreted in the ambient \(\operatorname{Fig}(E)\), the final list is insufficient. Without (B.P) on the atelier side, the forward equivalence is already false by Counterexample~\ref{SA21-B-M3}.

\label{SA21-B-Atstar-literal} Let \(E=\{a,b\}\), \(\mathscr U=\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}\), and \(\mathscr H=\{\varnothing,\mathscr U\}\). This contains the empty figure and is closed under bounded unions. The canonical principal subfigures agree wherever they occur. The only nontrivial inclusion of occurring strata is \(\{a\}\subset\{a,b\}\), and its canonical singleton figure refines \(\mathscr U\) in the ambient set-figure atelier. For the pair \(\mathscr U,\mathscr U\), the premise of At\(^*4\) fails at the stratum \(\{a\}\), whose canonical singleton is omitted; for pairs involving the empty figure the conclusion holds. Finally \(\mathscr U\) is an admissible separating cover, with residuals \(\{a\},\{b\}\). Thus the shortened literal conditions hold, but \(\widehat{\{a\}}=\{\{a\}\}\notin\mathscr H\). The figure poset has only one nonzero irreducible, so cannot recover the two prescribed ground objects.

\label{SA21-B-Cont-bridge} The final Cont 1--5 plus Fig 1--4 of 156-4/34--40, with the geometric-dimension clause retained and with transitivity of internal refinement added, are equivalent to the prime At 1--7 plus L1, D\(_0\) and that same dimension clause. The optional finite-principal clause Cont \(3'\) can be added on both sides. The transitivity addition cannot be omitted, even if Cont 6 and Cond 7 are imposed.

\label{SA21-B-Cont-counter} Use the two orders on \(\{p,q,z,u,t\}\) from Counterexample~\ref{SA21-B-missing-transitivity}, and specify compatibility independently as equality together with the three undirected pairs \(pq,qz,zt\). Take all clique downsets as figures. The only strict incidence is \(z<t\), and it is exactly compatible refinement. Compatibility is incidence-hereditary. All principal figures and all their closed subfigures occur; compatible unions occur. Every refinement has combinatorial dimension at most one. The open lieu sets listed earlier are nonempty and disjoint on the three compatible pairs. The only nonzero disjoint elementary pairs are \(p,q\) and \(q,z\); refining \(z\) can replace it by \(p\), so disjointness is hereditary. Thus final Cont 1--5 hold. Whole-shadow disjointness detects exactly those pairs, so Cont 6 holds; open lieux of compatible distinct strata are orthogonal, so Cond 7 holds. Nevertheless \(p\rho u\rho t\) and \(p\not\rho t\). The finite certificate checks all figures, carriers and refinement pairs; it also verifies prime At 1--6.

\label{SA21-B-C6-C8} Read C6(a) literally: for \(F'\preceq F\) and \(G\leq F\), there is exactly one \(H\) satisfying \(H\leq F'\) and \(H\preceq G\). Then \[ F\leq H\preceq F\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F=H \] for arbitrary figures, and both clauses of C8\(_0\) follow. With C7\(_0\), the derived relation \(P\ll F\Longleftrightarrow\exists H\ (P\leq H\preceq F)\) is a partial order.

\label{SA21-B-C-carriers} Let \(M=\{d,a,y,z\}\), with \(d<a,d<y,d<z\). Every pair is compatible except \(a,y\) and \(a,z\). The figures, written by their deployments, are \[ 0,\quad d,\quad da,\quad dy,\quad dz,\quad dyz. \] Primitive subdivision is equality together with \[ da\preceq dy,\qquad da\preceq dz,\qquad da\preceq dyz. \] This is a partial order. All nonempty figures contain \(d\), so no two are disjoint and C5 holds. C1--C3, including (B.P), are the explicit clique-downset construction. The incidence graph of \(M\) is connected, so C4 and C4 bis impose no additional condition. For \(da\preceq dy\) or \(da\preceq dz\), restriction sends the bottom, the subfigure \(d\), and the whole parent respectively to \(0,d,da\). For \(da\preceq dyz\), it sends \(0,d,dy,dz,dyz\) respectively to \(0,d,da,da,da\). These are the unique subfigures that subdivide the prescribed subfigure; they have exactly the strata refining it, and preserve all joins. Identity subdivisions restrict identically. This checks C6(a,b,c) completely. A subdivision \(da\preceq dy\leq dyz\) extends by \(da\preceq dyz\), and likewise for \(dz\); all other extension cases are identities. Hence C7\(_0\) holds, as does C8\(_0\). Nevertheless \(a\ll dyz\), and the strata refined by \(a\) in \(dyz\) are \(y,z\), with no least member. Thus the later At 5 fails. Final C8, the \emph{full gluing} axiom for subdivisions, is a different assertion and fails here: the subdivisions \(da\preceq dy\) and \(dz\preceq dz\) agree on \(d\) but cannot glue, because \(a,z\) are incompatible. The script \texttt{legacy\_subdivision.py} exhaustively checks all bounded joins, every C6 restriction and every C7\(_0\) extension.

\label{SA21-B-modern-C} Suppose a prime atelier has the carrier calculus, L1, L3, C, At supp, At 14, and gluing for the covers under consideration. Define subdivision by (B.S). Then it satisfies C1--C3, C5, literal C6(a,b,c), C7\(_0\), C8\(_0\), and subdivision gluing C8. The independent incidence-component axioms C4 and C4 bis are not consequences. In a full canonical figure family C4 implies C4 bis; for a restricted atlas it need not.

\label{SA21-B-C4bis} Take an infinite set of independent point objects, both orders equal to identity, and internal disjointness equal to inequality. Admit only finite figures. All the strong local axioms, finite gluing and At Fil hold; the latter holds because its parent has only finitely many strata, so local stationarity is joint stationarity. Every incidence component is one point and distinct components are compatible, so C4 holds. The family containing one point figure from every component has no figure union, so C4 bis fails. This failure concerns an unbounded family and is consistent with At Fil.

\label{SA21-B-primitive-not-support} There is a second reason not to identify primitive subdivision with (B.S) without an extra axiom. For the two-element incidence chain \(a<x\), with all downsets as figures and primitive subdivision equal to identity, C5, C6, C7\(_0\) and C8 hold tautologically. Derived refinement is incidence. Both nonempty figures have cosupport \(\{0\}\), so (B.S) would additionally declare \(a\preceq x\). C5 says that subdivisions preserve cosupport; it does not say every same-support refinement is one. The complete two-stratum structure, including every C6 restriction, C7 extension and C8 gluing assignment, is checked in \texttt{legacy\_subdivision.py}.

\label{SA21-B-spatial-separations} Strong Mag 1--4, even together with Mog L2 and all the extension existence axioms, do not force At spat 3. In the two-object model of Counterexample~\ref{SA21-B-extension-unique}, internal orthogonality is empty, so the orthoclosure of either singleton is \(M\). The two elementary deployments have the same single label \(M\) and the same one-point order. They therefore fail the required injectivity. Conversely the typed spatial axioms do not force divisibility. Take incidence \(a<t\), \(\rho=\mathrm{id}\), and \(\delta\) equal to inequality on \(\{a,t\}\). Orthoclosures are singletons. The two deployments are the labelled singleton \(\{\{a\}\}\) and the labelled chain \(\{a\}<\{t\}\); labels within a deployment are nonzero and orthogonal, and the deployments are distinct. A top-preserving carrier by inclusion of these singleton labels exists exactly for an identical source and target, recovering \(\rho=\mathrm{id}\). Thus the fully typed spatial axioms hold. The only lieu is \(a\), but \(U_t=\varnothing\), so divisibility fails. The finite certificate checks the orthoclosures and both deployment assertions.

\label{SA21-B-incidence-components} Let \(L\) be an arbitrary set. A multistrate in \(\operatorname{Fig}(L)\) is an elementary admissible family of subsets of \(L\), ordered by closed-subfamily incidence. If \(|L|\geq3\), the connected components of its comparability graph are exactly: \begin{enumerate} \item the isolated multistrate \(\{L\}\); \item for each \(p\in L\), the two-object component \[ \{L\setminus\{p\}\} \ <\ \{L\setminus\{p\},L\}; \] \item one component containing every remaining multistrate. \end{enumerate} The last component contains every point multistrate. For \(|L|=2\) there are just the isolated object and the two two-object components. For \(|L|=1\) there is one object and one component; for \(L=\varnothing\), there are no multistrates. Thus a finite \(n\)-point set has \(n+2\) components for \(n\geq3\), three for \(n=2\), one for \(n=1\), and none for \(n=0\).

\label{SA21-B-C4-false} For every set \(L\) with at least two elements, C4 fails in \(\operatorname{Fig}(L)\). The isolated object \(\{L\}\) and any point figure lie in different incidence components and are incompatible. Their underlying supports meet, while their common incidence subfigure is empty.

\label{SA21-B-figure-components} Let \(\Phi\) be any admissible family on \(L\), and let \(\pi:|\Phi|\to\Phi\) send a point to its least stratum. Give \(|\Phi|\) the Alexandrov topology whose closed sets are \(\pi^{-1}(D)\) for downsets \(D\subseteq\Phi\). Its connected components are exactly the inverse images of the comparability components of the stratum poset \(\Phi\). No finiteness hypothesis is needed. For a finite frontier stratification by definably connected cells, with each closed stratum the closure of its cell, these same components are exactly the definable connected components of its actual support. In particular this applies to the o-minimal cell atelier of Part B.4.

\label{SA21-B-refinement-components} Let \(\mathscr A\) be a set-theoretic atelier on \(L\), with inherited set-figure refinement, containing every point figure and closed under disjoint unions. Make a hypergraph on \(L\) whose hyperedges are the supports of the multistrates. The comparability components of \((M,\ll)\) are exactly the components of that support hypergraph, with a multistrate assigned to the component containing its support. Multistrates in different refinement components are compatible. For the full \(\operatorname{Fig}(L)\), the refinement graph is connected whenever \(L\ne\varnothing\). For the closed o-minimal cell atelier of Part B.4, its refinement components are exactly the definable connected components of the ambient definable set \(X\).

\label{SA21-BM-r12} The literal finite-figure axioms C1--C3 do not imply representation by finite downward-closed compatibility cliques. The failure persists after adding C4, C4 bis, and the C5--C8 subdivision axioms, including C8\(_0\), as stated in 156-4, scans 65--87.

\label{SA21-BM-event-iff} For a finite-figure system satisfying C1--C3, the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item Every principal ideal \(\mathcal F_{\leq F}\) is distributive. \item Every multistrate is prime for bounded joins. \item Deployment is an isomorphism of ordered sets \[ \mathcal F\cong \{A\subseteq M:A\text{ is finite, downward closed, and an }R \text{-clique}\}, \] where \(mRn\) means that \(m,n\) have a common upper bound. \item \(\mathcal F\) is the finite configuration poset of a binary-conflict prime event structure with finite causes. \end{enumerate} The event structure is recovered, uniquely up to a bijection preserving causality and conflict, by \[ E=M,\qquad \leq_E=\leq|_M,\qquad m\mathbin{\#}n\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg(mRn). \] These conditions identify the whole representable subclass of literal finite contrées. Adding C4 corresponds exactly to requiring all conflict to occur within undirected causality components. Adding C4 bis while retaining finite figures requires that there be only finitely many nonempty such components.
\label{SA21-BM-binary} Even after correcting R12 by local distributivity, the corresponding class is the binary-conflict class, not all prime event structures under the finite-consistency convention.

\label{SA21-BM-domain} For the corrected class, let \(\mathcal C_f(E)\) denote finite configurations and \(\mathcal C(E)\) all downward-closed conflict-free subsets. Then \[ \mathcal C(E)\cong\operatorname{Idl}(\mathcal C_f(E)), \] where ideals are nonempty directed downward-closed sets. The compact elements are the finite configurations, and the complete primes are \(\downarrow e\). This is the coherent prime-algebraic domain correspondence of \citet[Theorems 8--9, Definitions 17--18, p.~102]{NPW1981}. For the whole-figure disjointness of 156-4 set \[ e\perp_E f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \neg(e\#f)\text{ and }\downarrow e\cap\downarrow f=\varnothing. \] The support ortholattice of finite configurations is canonically isomorphic to the closed double polars of \((E,\perp_E)\), and to the support ortholattice using all configurations. This concerns whole-figure disjointness, not the later primitive internal disjointness. If the empty configuration is retained as an orthogonality vertex, it is universally self-orthogonal, and every closed figure polar contains it. Removing this one radical vertex gives the ordinary irreflexive orthoset convention and the same support ortholattice.

\label{SA21-BM-refinement} The event structure determines incidence, compatibility and the preceding whole-figure supports, but not refinement, subdivision, lieux, or primitive internal disjointness. Given multistrate refinement satisfying At 4, its translation is \[ g\ll f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall e\in g)(\exists d\in f)\ e\ll d . \] Under At 13, subdivision translates as \[ g\preceq f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g\ll f\text{ and }g^\perp=f^\perp, \] equivalently maximality for configuration inclusion among refinements of \(f\).

\label{SA21-BM-cell-calculus} The relations \(\leq,\ll\) are partial orders with \(\leq\subseteq\ll\). Refinement has a unique monotone carrier \[ c_{G,F}:\operatorname{Str}(G)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Str}(F), \qquad C_B\subseteq C_{c_{G,F}(B)}. \] For \(m\ll n\), the least substratum of \(n\) refined by \(m\) is its top-cell carrier. Consequently \[ m\ll^\circ n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\ll n\text{ and }m^\circ\subseteq n^\circ. \] Figures are compatible exactly when, after uniting their elementary subfigures, all distinct multistrates have disjoint top cells; the join is then that union. They are disjoint exactly when their supports are disjoint. For \(G\ll F\), \(H\leq F\), induced refinement is \[ G|H=\{B\in G:c_{G,F}(B)\in H\}, \qquad |G|H|=|G|\cap|H|. \]

\label{SA21-BM-cell-axioms} The chronological meanings of labels are fixed in Part B.1. Positive entries hold for every definable \(X\); negative entries mean failure for some such \(X\), proved below. \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{p{0.19\linewidth}p{0.57\linewidth}p{0.13\linewidth}} \hline System & Axioms & Value\\ \hline 156-4, Cont & Cont 1--5, Fig 1--4, finite geometric dimension, finite principal ideals, Cond 7--8 & True\\ 156-4, C & C1--C3, bounded-join primality, C5, C6, C7\(_0\), canonical extension, C8, C8\(_0\) & True\\ 156-4, C & Global incidence C4 and C4 bis & False\\ 156-6 & At 1--8, At 9, At \(9'\), At 10--13, At \(11'\), At 11 bis & True\\ 156-6 & At \(9_\Sigma\) for all finite posets & True\\ 156-6 & At \(9''\), or the empty/principal restriction in \(9_\Sigma\) & False\\ 156-6 & At 14, geometric At 14 bis, At 14 ter & True\\ 156-6 & Literal all-target reflection in At 14 bis & False\\ 156-7 & At C, At D, At D\(_0\), At CD, At CD2, At CD2\( '\), At L1--L3, CL(spac), CL(pol), At supp & True\\ 156-7 & At pol 1, At simp 1 & False\\ 156-8 & Mag 1--4, strong-refinement formulation, weaker primed clauses, Mog L1--L2, divisible-magasin clauses & True\\ 156-8 & Atlas At 1--5, At Fil & True\\ 156-9 & Renamed At 1--4, At spat 1--3 & True\\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{center} Geometric At 14 bis means the mixed incidence condition between a new boundary stratum and a stratum outside that boundary. The literal all-target reading of its uncertain transcription is treated separately below.

\label{SA21-BM-cell-support} The cell atelier is faithful and spatial. Its complete support ortholattice for primitive internal disjointness is \[ \Sigma_M\cong\mathcal P(X). \] The open support of \(m\) corresponds to \(m^\circ\), and its whole support to \(|m|\). This is the full powerset, not only the definable subsets.

\label{SA21-BM-cell-extension} If \(G\leq F\), \(G'\preceq G\), the closed-stratum family \[ E=G'\cup(F\setminus G) \] is a figure with \(E\preceq F\), \(E|G=G'\). Every other extension \(H\preceq F\) inducing \(G'\) refines \(E\), so \(E\) is the unique coarsest extension. Its carrier is an order isomorphism outside the prescribed boundary and has the required mixed incidences. Every extension with this complement property is equal to \(E\). For elementary \(m\), a subdivision of \(\partial m\) extends uniquely to an elementary \(m'\preceq m\) with that boundary. Thus At 14, geometric At 14 bis and At 14 ter hold.

\label{SA21-BM-14bis-reading} The literal mixed-order clause of 156-6, scan 88, as transcribed and visually checked in Part B.1, is false in the cell model if its second variable is allowed to range over all of \(\widetilde F'\). The corrected clause restricts that variable to \(\widetilde F'\setminus\widetilde G'\).

\label{SA21-BM-cell-moderation} Every finite collection of subdivisions of a cell figure has a common subdivision. Every closed definable \(S\subseteq X\) has a cell figure, and any finite collection of its finite cell stratifications has a common refinement. In particular the atelier is modérée in the sense of 156-4, scan 70.

\label{SA21-BM-cell-connected} The undirected refinement components of \((M,\ll)\) are exactly the definably connected components of \(X\): a multistrate is assigned the unique component containing its support, and two multistrates are in the same refinement component exactly when those assignments agree. Different refinement components are compatible. For an individual finite figure, its incidence components are exactly the definably connected components of its support.

\label{SA21-BM-cell-limits} Global incidence C4 and C4 bis, the polyhedral restrictions and an infinite-family strengthening of moderation fail in general. Allowing arbitrary nonclosed supports with closures taken only relative to themselves also destroys the disjoint-support compatibility axiom.

\label{SA21-C01} Let $M$ have a fixed-point-free involution. If an irreflexive relation $\perp\,\subseteq M\times M$ satisfies $x\perp y\Rightarrow a(x)\perp y$, then it cannot equal inequality unless $M=\varnothing$.

\label{SA21-C02} Suppose interior refinement is identity and disjunction is corrected to orbit inequality. If Magor~2(b) permits $X'\triangleleft X^\epsilon$ for either sign $\epsilon$ but concludes $X'\triangleleft Y$ with $Y=X$, then Magor~1, $1'$, 5 and 6 permit precisely the graphs whose edges are all loops; there are no cells of dimension at least two. If the target is given the same sign, or the source superscript is absent, Magor~2(b) is automatic and the general graph dictionary below applies.

\label{SA21-C03} Let $P$ be any poset and $B_x=P_{<x}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $B_x$ is nonempty and connected for either Alexandrov topology; \item its undirected comparability graph is connected; \item $|\Delta(B_x)|$ is nonempty and connected. \end{enumerate} If principal ideals are finite, the comparability graph can be replaced by the Hasse graph. Thus the exact additional incidence axiom for connected cell boundaries is that any two proper faces of each cell of dimension at least two can be joined by a finite incidence zigzag among its proper faces. Dimensions zero and one must be excepted.

\label{SA21-C04} In dimension at most one, oriented maquettes are precisely graphs given by vertices $V$, oriented edges $E$, a free reversal $e\mapsto e^-$ on $E$, and an origin map $s:E\to V$. In dimension at most two, the oriented edges below each selected two-cell orientation form a disjoint union of finite directed cycles and two-sided infinite directed paths, with each incident vertex used once as origin and once as terminus. If each cell has finitely many faces, only finite cycles occur.

\label{SA21-C05} Even in finite dimension two, connected boundaries and the exclusion of loops do not make an oriented maquette regular. With finite faces per cell, the exact dimension-at-most-two regular class additionally excludes using both orientations of an underlying edge in one two-cell boundary.

\label{SA21-C06} Finite signed diamonds, connected positive-dimensional cell boundaries, and connected vertex links in the order complex do not characterize regular CW face posets. There is a counterexample with $55$ unoriented cells, of maximal dimension three.
\label{SA21-C07} Connectedness of positive-dimensional global links is not necessary for a poset to be a regular CW face poset.

\label{SA21-C08} Let $M$ carry free reversal and an immediate incidence relation invariant under simultaneous reversal. Suppose the induced relation on orientation orbits generates a poset $P$. These data arise from a regular CW complex with oriented cells and distinguished positive zero-cell orientations if and only if the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item Every principal ideal of $P$ is finite. \item Immediate incidences project exactly to covers of $P$; for each cover $u<v$ and each orientation of $v$, exactly one orientation of $u$ is incident to it. \item For every $x\in P$, $|\Delta(P_{<x})|$ is homeomorphic to $S^{d(x)-1}$ for some integer $d(x)\ge0$. \item The products of the two incidence signs around every rank-two diamond are opposite; at an edge the two vertex coefficients have opposite signs relative to the distinguished vertex orientations. \end{enumerate} The spherical condition implies that the poset is graded and that $d(x)$ is its dimension rank. The theorem allows infinitely many cells, unbounded dimension, and failure of local finiteness. The empty case gives the empty CW complex.

\label{SA21-C09} For a poset $P$ of nonempty cells, let $P^0=P\cup\{0\}$ with a new minimum. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $P$ is the nonempty face poset of an abstract simplicial complex; \item every interval $[0,x]$ is a finite Boolean lattice and $P^0$ is a meet-semilattice; \item every interval $[0,x]$ is finite Boolean and the map $x\mapsto V_x$, where $V_x$ is the set of atoms below $x$, is injective. \end{enumerate} The equivalence of the first two conditions is stated by \citet[\S2.3, pp.~8--9]{Bjorner1984}.

\label{SA21-C10} For maquettes, At pol~1 (156-7/14) says exactly that $P^0$ is a meet-semilattice. Within the regular CW class, At simp~1 (156-7/15) is automatic. Their conjunction does not characterize simplices or simplicial complexes. The square is a finite counterexample. An exact replacement is At pol~1 together with finite Boolean principal ideals. Equivalently, one can require finite distributive principal augmented lattices together with At simp~1, retaining At pol~1.

\label{SA21-C11} For any poset $L$, the finite nonempty flags ordered by inclusion form the simplicial face poset of $\Delta(L)$. By contrast, the construction of 156-9/5--7 has vertex cells $a\in L$ and interval cells $I_{a,b}$ for $a<b$; its incidence maquette is the one-dimensional simplicial complex given by the comparability graph of $L$. Its finite prefigures are positional flags, and its finite figures are exactly those flags closed under adjoining the two endpoints of every interval they contain.

\label{SA21-C12} For an arbitrary Alexandrov poset, the map \[ \mu_L:|\Delta(L)|\longrightarrow L, \qquad \mu_L(p)=\min\operatorname{supp}(p), \] for the lower-open convention, is a weak homotopy equivalence: \citet[Theorem~2, p.~466; construction in \S5, p.~469]{McCord1966}. This includes infinite posets and complexes with the weak topology; see also \citet[Theorem~1.4.6 and Remark~1.4.16]{Barmak2011}. It is generally neither a homeomorphism nor a homotopy equivalence.

\label{A1-dimensions} We use orientation-preserving markings that preserve the peripheral classes and labelled boundary circles; boundary points may move during isotopy. The positive-boundary Teichm\"uller space of stable type $(g,n)$ has real dimension $6g-6+3n$. For a connected stable graph of total genus $g$ with $n$ legs, its normalized component moduli together with a nonzero complex tangent tensor at every edge have complex dimension $3g-3+n$. Adding $n$ external positive cap parameters gives real dimension $6g-6+3n$. These counts verify 67/077 and 67/016, but do not establish existence or surjectivity of the proposed arrows.

\label{A1-cap-bound} Let $f:\D\longrightarrow\C\setminus\{1\}$ be injective and holomorphic, with $f(0)=0$. Then $|f'(0)|\leq4$. Thus a pointed disc in $\mathbf P^1$ centred at $0$ and avoiding $1,\infty$ has conformal radius at most $4$ in the coordinate $z$.

\label{A1-tensor} Let $f:\overline\D\to D_a\subset Y$ and $h:\overline\D\to D_b\subset Y$ parametrize two pointed analytic discs, with centres $a,b$. An orientation-reversing toric identification of their boundaries has the form $f(\zeta)\sim h(c/\zeta)$, $|\zeta|=1$, where $|c|=1$. Its tangent tensor is \[ q=c\,df_0(\partial_\zeta)\otimes dh_0(\partial_\eta). \] In any chosen branch coordinates its modulus is the product of the two conformal radii.

\label{A1-global-refutation} With the unrestricted nonzero-tensor target of cote 67/075--078, the proposed global isomorphisms are false. For the geodesic-cut interpretation the unbordered map is not surjective on complex objects, already for $(g,n)=(0,4)$ and then for every stable type with $3g-3+n>0$. The same cap-size obstruction rules out a preimage for specified bordered target objects whenever the tensor is obtained from the actual caps. This is an obstruction to coarse surjectivity as well as to equivalence of stacks or groupoids. Under the external-only admissibility reading the bordered arrow also has the separate failure of being undefined on some objects, proved in Proposition~\ref{A1-bordered-landing}; it must not be described simply as a globally defined map with a proper image. For arbitrary embedded cuts, Proposition~\ref{A1-nontoric-cut} supplies the earlier failure of the tensor construction itself.

\label{A1-zero} For $(g,n)=(0,3)$ there is no essential stable cut. The unbordered groupoid with labelled markings is a point.
